basins.name: Permian Basin
basins.crude_character: light sweet tight oil (WTI Midland area)
basins.source: EIA, Today in Energy, 2026-03-31: U.S. crude oil production rose in 2025 (STEO-based regional split)
basins.basis: direct published regional figure

basins.name: Bakken (Williston Basin)
basins.crude_character: light sweet tight oil
basins.source: North Dakota Industrial Commission / Department of Mineral Resources monthly production (Bakken + Three Forks, North Dakota portion), reported 2026-10-20
basins.basis: direct published regional figure; North Dakota portion only - the smaller Montana/South Dakota Bakken is excluded, so this understates the full basin slightly

basins.name: Eagle Ford
basins.crude_character: light sweet to condensate-rich tight oil
basins.source: EIA, Today in Energy, 2026-03-31 (STEO-based regional split, published rounded to 1.2 million b/d)
basins.basis: direct published regional figure, rounded as published

basins.name: DJ Basin (Niobrara)
basins.crude_character: light tight oil, gas-rich in the north
basins.source: Colorado state crude production, Energy & Carbon Management Commission data as reported 2026 (June 2026: 445 kb/d)
basins.basis: country/state split, approximate: DJ Basin output is effectively the Colorado state total; small non-DJ Colorado volumes are included

basins.name: Powder River Basin
basins.crude_character: light tight oil (Niobrara/Mowry/Turner)
basins.source: EIA Petroleum Supply Monthly state data (Wyoming 2025: 290 kb/d), released 2026-03-06
basins.basis: country/state split, approximate: basin figure proxied by the Wyoming state total, which is dominated by Powder River Basin output

basins.name: Anadarko Basin (incl. SCOOP/STACK)
basins.crude_character: light tight oil and condensate
basins.source: EIA Petroleum Supply Monthly state data (Oklahoma 2025: 405 kb/d), released 2026-03-06
basins.basis: country/state split, approximate: basin figure proxied by the Oklahoma state total, which is dominated by Anadarko Basin / SCOOP-STACK output

basins.name: Gulf of Mexico (federal offshore)
basins.crude_character: medium sour offshore crude (Mars blend area)
basins.source: EIA, Today in Energy, 2026-03-31; cross-checked against EIA August 2026 STEO reporting federal Gulf output near 1.98 million b/d forecast for 2026
basins.basis: direct published regional figure

basins.name: Alaska North Slope
basins.crude_character: medium crude (ANS), declining legacy fields plus new Pikka/Nuna volumes
basins.source: EIA Petroleum Supply Monthly state data (Alaska 2025: 421 kb/d); cross-check: EIA STEO forecast of 477 kb/d for 2026 (EIA, 2025-11-19)
basins.basis: country/state split, approximate: North Slope is the bulk of Alaska output; a small Cook Inlet volume is included in the state total

basins.name: WCSB oil sands - mining
basins.crude_character: extra-heavy bitumen, upgraded to synthetic crude and sold as non-upgraded bitumen/dilbit
basins.source: Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) production data, July 2025 mined bitumen average, via Oil Sands Magazine AER round-up 2025-09-12
basins.basis: direct published regional figure (AER, via trade press round-up of the AER release)

basins.name: WCSB oil sands - in situ (thermal)
basins.crude_character: extra-heavy bitumen (SAGD/CSS), diluted for export as dilbit
basins.source: Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) production data, July 2025 in-situ average (a monthly record in that release), via Oil Sands Magazine AER round-up 2025-09-12
basins.basis: direct published regional figure (AER, via trade press round-up of the AER release)

basins.name: WCSB conventional (Alberta)
basins.crude_character: conventional light/medium and heavy crude plus pentanes
basins.source: AER data compiled by Oil Sands Magazine (updated 2026-10-07): Alberta conventional light+medium 399 kb/d + conventional heavy 173 kb/d, Jan-Aug 2026
basins.basis: direct published provincial split; Saskatchewan and BC conventional volumes are not in this Alberta-only figure

basins.name: West Siberia
basins.crude_character: medium sour crude (Urals blend feedstock)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: structural share of Russian output from EIA Russia country analysis (Khanty-Mansi / West Siberia is about half of Russian production) applied to the EIA June 2026 Russian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - no basin-level Russian series is published openly; share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Volga-Urals
basins.crude_character: medium sour crude
basins.source: Country split, approximate: structural Volga-Urals share (Tatarstan/Bashkortostan, roughly a tenth of Russian output, per EIA Russia country analysis) applied to the EIA June 2026 Russian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Sakhalin (Far East offshore)
basins.crude_character: light sweet offshore crude (Sokol/Vityaz blends)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: Sakhalin-1/-2 structural share of Russian output applied to the EIA June 2026 Russian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Saudi Eastern Province (Ghawar)
basins.crude_character: light crude (Arab Light feedstock) from the world's largest onshore field
basins.source: Published field profiles citing Saudi Aramco disclosures (Ghawar producing capacity about 3.8 million b/d, 2025 profiles)
basins.basis: approximate field figure: Aramco does not publish a monthly Ghawar series; 2026 national output was disruption-cut (see countries.json), so this is a pre-disruption capacity-era figure, not a June 2026 read

basins.name: Kuwait - Burgan
basins.crude_character: medium crude (Kuwait Export Crude feedstock) from the Greater Burgan field
basins.source: Published field profiles of Greater Burgan (capacity roughly 1.6-1.7 million b/d)
basins.basis: approximate field figure: KPC does not publish a monthly Burgan series; national 2026 output was disruption-cut (see countries.json)

basins.name: Iraq south (Rumaila / West Qurna)
basins.crude_character: medium/heavy sour crude (Basrah grades)
basins.source: Sum of published field figures: Rumaila about 1,450 kb/d (published operator/ministry profiles, approximate), West Qurna 1 550 kb/d (Global Energy Monitor field table: 200.75 million bbl in 2024), West Qurna 2 about 400 kb/d (operator reporting, 2026)
basins.basis: approximate sum of published field figures, mixed vintages; EIA notes a break in its Iraq national series in 2026 (see countries.json), so treat as a scale figure, not a current-month read

basins.name: UAE onshore (Murban / Bab)
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude (Murban)
basins.source: ADNOC onshore (Murban) production-capacity disclosures and published profiles, 2025
basins.basis: approximate: ADNOC publishes capacity by grade, not a monthly onshore series

basins.name: Iran southwest (Khuzestan / Ahwaz)
basins.crude_character: medium/heavy sour crude (Iran Heavy feedstock)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: Khuzestan fields are roughly two-thirds of Iranian crude output (structural share in published country analyses) applied to the EIA June 2026 Iranian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Pre-Caspian (Tengiz + Kashagan)
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude (CPC Blend / Kashagan grades)
basins.source: Field reporting via BOE Report, April 2026: Tengiz 973 kb/d + Kashagan 414 kb/d
basins.basis: direct published field figures, summed; note the July 2026 CPC disruption cut Tengiz output sharply that month (Reuters, industry source), so April is a pre-disruption read

basins.name: Libya - Sirte Basin
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude (Es Sider / Sarir area grades)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: Sirte Basin structural share (roughly two-thirds of Libyan output) applied to the EIA June 2026 Libyan total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Algeria - Hassi Messaoud
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude (Saharan Blend feedstock)
basins.source: Published field profiles of Hassi Messaoud (output roughly 350-450 kb/d)
basins.basis: approximate field figure: Sonatrach does not publish a monthly field series

basins.name: Nigeria - Niger Delta (onshore + deepwater)
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude onshore (Bonny Light area); medium sweet deepwater grades (Egina/Bonga area)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: essentially all Nigerian production is Niger Delta onshore/shallow plus deepwater offshore the delta; figure is about 85% of the EIA June 2026 Nigerian total-liquids read in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Angola deepwater (Blocks 17/31/32 area)
basins.crude_character: medium sweet deepwater crude (Girassol/Plutonio area grades)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: deepwater fields are roughly 90% of Angolan output (structural share in published country analyses) applied to the EIA June 2026 Angolan total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Brazil pre-salt (Santos + Campos)
basins.crude_character: medium sweet, low-sulfur pre-salt crude (Buzios/Tupi/Mero)
basins.source: ANP (Brazil regulator) monthly production bulletin for August 2026, as reported 2026-10-01: pre-salt oil 3,842 kb/d from 203 wells, 82.6% of national oil+gas output
basins.basis: direct published regional figure (ANP)

basins.name: Venezuela - Orinoco Belt
basins.crude_character: extra-heavy crude, upgraded or diluted for export
basins.source: PDVSA sources quoted by Reuters (February 2026 Orinoco Belt output just over 500 kb/d), as reported 2026
basins.basis: direct published regional figure as reported; Venezuelan official data is not independently verified - treat as the operator-stated read

basins.name: Mexico offshore Campeche (incl. Ku-Maloob-Zaap)
basins.crude_character: heavy sour crude (Maya feedstock)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: the Campeche offshore (Ku-Maloob-Zaap, Abkatun, Litoral de Tabasco) is the large majority of Mexican crude output in Pemex reporting; figure is an approximate share of the EIA June 2026 Mexican total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Colombia - Llanos Basin
basins.crude_character: medium/heavy crude (Castilla/Rubiales area)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: Llanos is roughly 70% of Colombian output (structural share in regulator/ANH reporting) applied to the EIA June 2026 Colombian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: Argentina - Vaca Muerta (Neuquen Basin)
basins.crude_character: light sweet shale oil (Medanito area)
basins.source: Argentina Energy Secretariat data for September 2026 (Vaca Muerta 698.5 kb/d, 71.7% of the national record total of 973.7 kb/d), reported 2026-10
basins.basis: direct published regional figure (national energy secretariat)

basins.name: Guyana - Stabroek Block (offshore)
basins.crude_character: light sweet offshore crude (Liza/Payara/Yellowtail grades)
basins.source: Guyana government production data / ExxonMobil reporting: four FPSOs producing about 900 kb/d through Q2 2026 (903 kb/d in April 2026 on government data)
basins.basis: direct published regional figure; essentially all Guyanese production is the Stabroek Block. A fifth FPSO (Uaru, 250 kb/d design) was due to start in Q4 2026, after this vintage

basins.name: North Sea - Norway sector
basins.crude_character: medium sweet offshore crude (incl. Johan Sverdrup, the largest single field)
basins.source: Norwegian Offshore Directorate (NOD) production data, in-stack pull: August 2026 oil 1,875 kb/d (final). Cross-check: Johan Sverdrup alone ran about 690 kboe/d in H1 2026 (operator/partner reporting)
basins.basis: direct published national figure (NOD); Norwegian output is essentially all offshore North Sea / Norwegian Sea / Barents Sea

basins.name: North Sea - UK sector
basins.crude_character: light/medium offshore crude (Forties/Brent area blends)
basins.source: North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) data: UK offshore oil production 456 kb/d in July 2026, down 21% year on year, as reported 2026-10
basins.basis: direct published regional figure (NSTA)

basins.name: Azerbaijan - ACG (offshore Caspian)
basins.crude_character: light sweet crude (Azeri Light, via BTC)
basins.source: BP reporting for Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG produced roughly 360 kb/d in recent BP annual/quarterly reporting)
basins.basis: approximate field figure from operator reporting; ACG is the large majority of Azerbaijani oil output

basins.name: Malaysia offshore (Peninsular / Sabah / Sarawak)
basins.crude_character: light sweet offshore crude (Tapis area)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: essentially all Malaysian production is offshore; figure is the EIA June 2026 Malaysian total-liquids read in countries.json, rounded down for small onshore/other volumes
basins.basis: country split, approximate - total is published

basins.name: Indonesia legacy (Sumatra / Java Sea)
basins.crude_character: medium crude, waxy in parts (Minas/Duri area)
basins.source: Country split, approximate: legacy Sumatra and Java Sea fields are roughly 70% of Indonesian output (structural share in published country analyses) applied to the EIA June 2026 Indonesian total in countries.json
basins.basis: country split, approximate - share labelled, total is published

basins.name: China - Daqing
basins.crude_character: medium crude, high wax, very mature waterflood/polymer flood
basins.source: CNPC/Xinhua reporting of Daqing crude output held near the 30 million tonne per year plateau (30 Mt/yr is about 600 kb/d)
basins.basis: approximate: converted from the published tonnes-per-year plateau; no monthly field series is published openly

basins.name: China - Changqing (Ordos Basin)
basins.crude_character: light tight oil and conventional crude
basins.source: CNPC reporting of Changqing oil output (roughly 24-25 million tonnes per year of oil within a roughly 60 Mt oil-equivalent total)
basins.basis: approximate: converted from published tonnes-per-year figures; oil-only split of an oil+gas total, labelled approximate

basins.name: China - Bohai Bay offshore
basins.crude_character: medium/heavy offshore crude

global_pipelines.name: Druzhba — Northern Branch
global_pipelines.flow_note: Scope-limited MEASURED: Kazakh crude delivered to Germany via Adamowo-Zastawa was 1.5 Mt in 2024 (KazMunayGas via Interfax/Reuters) = 1.5e6 t x 7.33 bbl/t / 365 = ~30 kbd on the Poland-Germany leg. This excludes Belarus domestic offtake west of the split, for which no clean 2024 branch total was found, so it understates total northern-branch flow. Russian crude on this leg stopped in 2023.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia/GEM Druzhba (system 5,100 km, 1,400 kbd total); Interfax/KMG 2024 Germany deliveries 1.5 Mt

global_pipelines.name: Druzhba — Southern Branch
global_pipelines.flow_note: Ukraine transit of Russian oil via the southern branch was 11.36 Mt in 2024 (former Ukrainian energy minister Olga Buslavets, reported by Interfax 20 Jan 2025) = ~228 kbd. Cross-check: Vedomosti via Reuters put it at 11.5 Mt (~230 kbd), split Hungary 4.8 / Slovakia 4.0 / Czechia 2.7 Mt. A third secondary source gave 9.7 Mt for Hungary+Slovakia only, inconsistent with the country split above; the Interfax/Vedomosti figures agree and are used.
global_pipelines.source: Interfax 2025-01-20 (11.36 Mt, 2024); Reuters/Vedomosti 2025-02-07 (11.5 Mt); Wikipedia Druzhba route via Mozyr/Uzhgorod

global_pipelines.name: Baltic Pipeline System (BPS-1) — to Primorsk
global_pipelines.flow_note: Terminal-proxy MEASURED: Transneft reported Primorsk crude loadings of 44.4 Mt in 2023 (TASS via Reuters/Hellenic Shipping News) = ~892 kbd. This is port loadings fed by BPS-1, not a pipeline meter reading; it includes transit volumes. Transneft said 57 Mt was 'realistic' for 2024, which would imply ~1,145 kbd, but that was a forecast, not a reported outturn, so the 2023 reported figure is used.
global_pipelines.source: Transneft via Reuters/TASS Jan 2024 (Primorsk 44.4 Mt 2023); GEM/Wikipedia BPS capacity ~75 Mtpa

global_pipelines.name: Baltic Pipeline System-2 (BPS-2) — to Ust-Luga
global_pipelines.flow_note: Terminal-proxy MEASURED: Transneft reported Ust-Luga crude loadings of 34 Mt in 2023, up 9% (TASS via Reuters) = ~683 kbd. Port loadings fed by BPS-2, not a pipeline meter reading. Capacity conflicts in sources: GEM 1,000 kbd / 50 Mtpa design vs 30 Mtpa phase-1 and 38 Mtpa phase-2 figures in Transneft/PortNews releases; the higher design figure is carried and the conflict is noted.
global_pipelines.source: GEM BPS-2 (1,170 km, 1,000 kbd); Offshore Technology BPS-2 (50 Mtpa); Transneft via Reuters Jan 2024 (Ust-Luga 34 Mt 2023)

global_pipelines.name: Tikhoretsk–Novorossiysk (incl. Grozny–Tikhoretsk feed)
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED, weakest line in the set: no clean public capacity or throughput for the Tikhoretsk-Novorossiysk trunk itself was found after hunting Transneft/Chernomortransneft material. Flow set at 300 kbd as a conservative assumed anchor, roughly half of Transneft's reported Novorossiysk (Sheskharis, non-CPC) loadings of 30 Mt in 2023 (~602 kbd), on the stated basis that this trunk is the main but not the only feed. Do not treat as measured.
global_pipelines.source: Transneft via Reuters Jan 2024 (Novorossiysk 30 Mt 2023, Sheskharis); route towns from Chernomortransneft system descriptions / Wikipedia

global_pipelines.name: Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED: CPC shipped 63.01 Mt through the system in 2024 (CPC/Interfax, Oct 2025 release; KMG 2024 annual report gives 55.7 Mt of Kazakh oil within that total) = ~1,265 kbd. Cross-checks: 48.48 Mt in Jan-Sep 2024 and 63.47 Mt in 2023, both CPC-reported. Capacity: 67 Mtpa nameplate (~1,340 kbd), debottlenecked toward 72.5-83 Mtpa; 1,400 kbd carried.
global_pipelines.source: CPC via Interfax (63.01 Mt in 2024); KMG Annual Report 2024; GEM CPC (1,511 km, 67 Mtpa)

global_pipelines.name: Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan (BTC)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED: BTC pumped 29.471 Mt in 2024, down 2.4% y/y, 82% Azerbaijani oil (Azerbaijan State Statistics via Interfax, Mar 2025) = ~592 kbd. Cross-checks: BP reported 22 Mt lifted at Ceyhan in Jan-Sep 2024, and BOTAS reported 228.8 Mbbl exported in 2023 (~627 kbd). Capacity conflicts: design 1,000 kbd, GEM lists 1,200 kbd after drag-reducer expansion; 1,200 carried.
global_pipelines.source: Interfax/Az Stat (29.471 Mt 2024); BP Azerbaijan Q3 2024 report; GEM BTC (1,768 km, 1,200 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: Baku–Supsa (Western Route Export Pipeline, WREP)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED but contested: BP reporting via GEM/AInvest states the line 'carried 1 million tons of oil in 2024' despite regular operations being suspended since spring 2022 = ~20 kbd. Conflict noted: Wikipedia's 2024 summary says reported estimates for 2024 vary and gives only ~150 kt for 2023. Treat the 20 kbd as a low-confidence measured figure; status is effectively intermittent spot shipments, not regular service.
global_pipelines.source: GEM Baku-Supsa / AInvest BP operatorship notice (1 Mt in 2024); Wikipedia Baku-Supsa (833 km, 145 kbd, suspended 2022)

global_pipelines.name: Baku–Novorossiysk (Northern Route Export Pipeline)
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: capacity 5 Mtpa (~100 kbd). No 2023-24 reported throughput was found; GEM notes loading 'has not exceeded 3 Mtpa in recent years' and only 824 kt was carried in 2019. Flow assumed at 0.4 x capacity = 40 kbd, consistent with that sub-3-Mtpa ceiling. The old CRS/EIA table giving 100-120 kbd as capacity is a capacity figure, not a flow, and is not used as one.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia/GEM Baku-Novorossiysk (1,330 km, 5 Mtpa); GEM background on recent loadings <3 Mtpa and 824 kt in 2019

global_pipelines.name: Atyrau–Samara (Uzen–Atyrau–Samara)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (operator segment total): KazTransOil reported 10.378 Mt transported on the Atyrau-Samara section in 2024 = ~208 kbd. Conflict noted: KMG's export-destination table gives 8.8 Mt of Kazakh exports via Atyrau-Samara in 2024; the difference is scope (operator section total vs Kazakh export origin only). The operator total is used for a pipeline-flow dataset. Capacity 310 kbd from EIA/CRS Caspian table; length for the Atyrau-Samara section is approximate (full Uzen-Atyrau-Samara system is longer).
global_pipelines.source: KazTransOil 2024 results release (10.378 Mt); KMG Annual Report midstream table (8.8 Mt export scope); EIA/CRS Caspian pipelines table (310 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: Transalpine Pipeline (TAL)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (terminal intake proxy): SIOT-TAL discharged 40.2 Mt at Trieste in 2024 with 423 tankers (SIOT via AdriaPorts, Feb 2026; 41.6 Mt in 2025) = ~807 kbd. Trieste intake is the TAL trunk's inflow, so it is a close proxy for trunk flow, but it is a port figure, not a pipeline meter. Capacity: GEM 850 kbd; Wikipedia 43 Mtpa (~860 kbd) — consistent.
global_pipelines.source: SIOT-TAL via AdriaPorts 2026-02-17 (40.2 Mt in 2024); GEM TAL (753 km, 850 kbd); Wikipedia TAL (43 Mtpa)

global_pipelines.name: Adria Pipeline (JANAF)
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.35 x 480 kbd rated capacity = 168 kbd. Capacity itself is contested: JANAF/MOL capacity tests in 2025-26 cite 11.4-14.3 Mtpa sustainable to the Hungarian border (~230-290 kbd), older industry sources rate the system at 400-480 kbd, and JANAF states 24 Mtpa technical capacity in Croatia. The only hard reported volume found was the ~2.1 Mt/yr JANAF contract to MOL's Hungarian and Slovak refineries (~42 kbd), which is a contract slice, not system flow, so no MEASURED upgrade was justified. Highest historical transport cited in the capacity-test debate is only ~2.2 Mt/yr, which suggests even this assumed figure may be generous — flagged as a weak line.
global_pipelines.source: GEM/JANAF system data; Hellenic Shipping News/IHS (480 kbd rating); JANAF-MOL capacity-test reporting 2025-26 (11.4-14.3 Mtpa tested, 2.1 Mt MOL contract)

global_pipelines.name: South European Pipeline (SPSE)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED but old vintage: SPSE/Wikipedia, citing the operator, gives maximum discharge 35 Mtpa and 'real used annual amount approximately 23 Mt/year' = ~462 kbd. That used-amount figure dates from around 2011 and no newer operator throughput was found; refinery closures on the route (Reichstett, Feyzin crude unit) mean current flow is very likely lower. Carried as measured with its vintage stated, not as a 2024 figure. System length 1,848 km includes branches; 769 km is the Fos-Karlsruhe main line used for the path.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia SPSE citing operator (35 Mtpa max, ~23 Mt/yr used, c.2011); SPSE company data

global_pipelines.name: SUMED Pipeline
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.5 x 2,500 kbd capacity = 1,250 kbd. Hunt result: EIA's chokepoint series now reports Suez Canal + SUMED combined only (total oil 8.8 MMb/d in 2023, 4.8 in 2024, crude+condensate 4.5 / 3.0), so a clean SUMED-only split could not be extracted and no MEASURED upgrade was justified. Last clean SUMED-only figure found is 1.1 MMb/d in 2009 (Wikipedia citing operator data). The 0.5 utilisation is a stated assumption, broadly consistent with that history.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia/GEM SUMED (320 km, 2,500 kbd, 1.1 MMb/d in 2009); EIA World Oil Transit Chokepoints (Suez+SUMED combined series)

global_pipelines.name: Kirkuk–Ceyhan (Iraq–Turkiye Pipeline)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (restart rate): flows resumed 27 Sep 2025 after the Mar 2023 arbitration shutdown and were running at ~180 kbd in early Oct 2025 (Reuters shipping sources via Baird Maritime; Iraq Oil Ministry agreement figure 180-190 kbd, planned ramp to 230 kbd). Pre-shutdown the line carried 400-450 kbd. Capacity conflicts: Wikipedia 1,500 kbd (1,100 + 500 twin lines), other sources 1,600-1,650 kbd; 1,600 carried. Status reflects a restarted but still ramping line.
global_pipelines.source: Reuters Oct 2025 restart reporting; Argus Sep-Oct 2025; Wikipedia Kirkuk-Ceyhan (970 km, 1,500 kbd design)

global_pipelines.name: Saudi East–West Pipeline (Petroline)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED: flow taken from the published baseline-utilisation figure of ~2.4 MMb/d used in KAPSARC's Hormuz-closure modelling and repeated in EIA-derived bypass summaries (normal use for Red Sea terminals plus west-coast refineries). That is a modelled baseline, not an operator meter reading, hence MODELLED not MEASURED. Capacity conflicts sharply: historic design 5,000 kbd vs Aramco's reported expansion to 7,000 kbd; 7,000 carried as nameplate, with Yanbu export-terminal capacity (~4.5-5.0 MMb/d per Kpler) the real ceiling. Low-quality 2026 reports claiming a ramp to 7,000 kbd in Q1 were found and discarded.
global_pipelines.source: KAPSARC Hormuz study (2.4 MMb/d baseline); EIA Hormuz bypass summaries; Kpler Beyond Hormuz (7,000 kbd pipe, ~4.5-5.0 MMb/d port ceiling)

global_pipelines.name: Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED: flow derived from published utilisation ranges — IEA-derived summaries put normal use at ~1.1 MMb/d and pre-crisis reporting at ~0.9 MMb/d (roughly half of upgraded capacity); 1,000 kbd is the midpoint of that published range, stated as a modelled figure, not a meter reading. Capacity conflicts: 1,500 kbd nameplate (ADNOC/EIA) vs ~1,800 kbd upgraded (multiple 2026 reports, and Kpler recorded 1.82 MMb/d of Fujairah loadings in Apr 2026 during the Hormuz disruption — an exceptional month, not a normal flow, so it was not used as the flow).
global_pipelines.source: EIA/IEA Hormuz bypass summaries (~1.1 MMb/d normal use); Kpler Beyond Hormuz (1.5 MMb/d nameplate, 1.82 MMb/d Apr 2026 loadings)

global_pipelines.name: Iraqi Pipeline in Saudi Arabia (IPSA)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED zero: the line has been out of operation since 1990 (GEM, citing the Gulf-crisis closure; Saudi Arabia confiscated its section in 2001 and later planned conversion of part to gas service). Flow is therefore a reported-status zero, not an assumption. Capacity 1,650 kbd and length 1,568 km from GEM.
global_pipelines.source: GEM IPSA (1,568 km, 1,650 kbd, mothballed, out of operation since 1990); Energy Intelligence 2005 on Saudi conversion plans

global_pipelines.name: Goreh–Kharg Pipeline (Iran Kharg feeders)
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED, weak line: no public capacity or throughput for the Goreh-Kharg feeder system itself was found (Iranian pipeline data is not published in the open sources searched). Flow assumed at 700 kbd on the stated basis that Kharg Island handles the large majority of Iran's crude exports, which were themselves only estimable from tanker tracking in the sources found. Length is the approximate onshore-plus-subsea feeder distance and is the weakest route geometry in the set. Treat as a placeholder, not a measurement.
global_pipelines.source: Route from public Iran terminal/field geography (Goreh pump station to Kharg terminal); no operator throughput published — see notes

global_pipelines.name: Trans Niger Pipeline (TNP)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (reported floor): BusinessDay reported crude transported through TNP had risen to 'more than 200,000 b/d in the last 6 months' as of early 2024, after ~460 illegal connections were removed in Apr 2023. 200 kbd is used as a floor, not a precise average. Note the Mar 2025 Bodo explosion subsequently disrupted the line, so this is a 2023-24 vintage figure.
global_pipelines.source: BusinessDay NG 2024 (TNP >200 kbd, ~180 km, >450 kbd capacity); SPDC/Renaissance operator reporting via press

global_pipelines.name: Trans Forcados Pipeline
global_pipelines.from: Odidi / western Niger Delta fields, Nigeria
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.58 x capacity, rounded to 140 kbd. Capacity conflicts in sources: Wikipedia 200-240 kbd for the 87 km 48-inch line, Heritage Energy (OML 30) describes the wider Trans-Forcados system at ~600 kbd, and an older account gives 850 kbd for the full system including feeders. The 240 kbd single-line figure is carried and the system figures are noted as a conflict. No reported 2023-25 throughput for the line itself was found.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia Trans Forcados (87 km, 200-240 kbd); Heritage Energy OML 30 / Trans-Forcados system descriptions (~600 kbd system)

global_pipelines.name: Haoud El Hamra–Arzew (OZ1/OZ2), Algeria
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: combined OZ1 (11 Mtpa, 801 km, 1965) + OZ2 (34 Mtpa, 821 km, 2005) capacity 45 Mtpa = ~900 kbd; flow assumed at 0.7 x combined capacity = 630 kbd. No Sonatrach line-level throughput was found in the open sources searched (Sonatrach publishes system totals, ~145 Mt liquids capacity, not line flows).
global_pipelines.source: GEM Haoud El Hamra-Arzew (OZ1 11 Mtpa / OZ2 34 Mtpa, 801 / 821 km); Sonatrach system descriptions

global_pipelines.name: Haoud El Hamra–Skikda (OK1), Algeria
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: capacity 30 Mtpa (GEM; corroborated by a 2006 US diplomatic cable describing the 645 km Haoud el-Hamra-Skikda oil line at 30 Mt/yr) = ~600 kbd; flow assumed at 0.7 x capacity = 420 kbd. No line-level reported throughput found.
global_pipelines.source: GEM Haoud El Hamra-Skikda (646 km, 30 Mtpa, 1972); Wikileaks cable 06ALGIERS1961 (645 km, 30 Mt/yr)

global_pipelines.name: Waha–Es Sider Pipeline, Libya
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow set at 300 kbd, Waha Oil's reported 'normal daily level' of production in restart reporting (Waha via press, after a 32-inch line repair returned ~200 kbd that had been shut in). That production level is an anchor, not a pipeline meter reading, so the basis stays ASSUMED. Terminal capacity at Es Sider is reported at over 400 kbd; Waha's own capacity is stated at more than 300 kbd by NOC. Route length is approximate — a replacement 700 km, 1,000 kbd line from the southern fields to Es Sider was reported by MEED in Nov 2025 as planned for tender in 2026, which is a new-build project, not the existing line, and is not used for capacity.
global_pipelines.source: Waha Oil / NOC via press (normal level ~300 kbd, 200 kbd restored on repair); MEED Nov 2025 (planned 700 km replacement, not existing capacity)

global_pipelines.name: El Sharara–Zawiya / Mellitah Pipeline, Libya
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.7 x 350 kbd = 245 kbd. The 350 kbd figure is both the Sharara field capacity and the Zawiya terminal's reported export capacity in NOC/logistics summaries; no line-level throughput was found. Sharara is routinely shut by blockades, so any single-year actual would differ materially — status reflects that history.
global_pipelines.source: NOC logistics summaries via APS/The Free Library (Sharara 350 kbd, Zawiya >350 kbd export capacity)

global_pipelines.name: Sarir–Tobruk (Marsa El Hariga) Pipeline, Libya
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED, weak line: no reliable public capacity or throughput for the Sarir-Tobruk trunk was found in the hunt. Flow assumed at 120 kbd as a stated placeholder anchored on Sarir being one of Libya's larger fields feeding the Hariga terminal, whose loading capacity is reported in tonnes/hour rather than a daily pipeline rate. Capacity left null rather than invented.
global_pipelines.source: NOC terminal summaries (Marsa El Hariga berths/loading rate); route from public Libyan field/terminal geography

global_pipelines.name: Chad–Cameroon Pipeline
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED: flow derived from Chad's published oil balance — total Chad production of roughly 130-150 kbd in recent EIA/OPEC reporting, almost all of it Doba crude exported via this line (Cameroon reported 47 Mbbl transited in 2019, ~129 kbd, per Societe Nationale des Hydrocarbures via GEM). 120 kbd is the modelled export share, not a current-year meter reading; no 2023-25 operator throughput was found.
global_pipelines.source: GEM Chad-Cameroon (1,070 km, 225 kbd; 47 Mbbl in 2019 per Cameroon SNH); EIA Chad production background

global_pipelines.name: Greater Nile Oil Pipeline
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (disrupted outturn, with a capacity conflict): Poten & Partners, citing tanker/export data, reported Bashayer exports fell from 195 kbd in Jan 2024 to 63 kbd in Apr 2024 after a rupture on this line in the Sudan war zone; 63 kbd is the last reported disrupted rate found, not a normal flow. Capacity conflict is material: EIA gives the Heglig-Port Sudan section a 450 kbd design capacity, while GEM lists the pipeline at 250 kbd — 450 is carried as design, 250 is likely the practical/derated figure. Both this line and Petrodar load at Bashayer, so terminal exports cannot be cleanly split between them; this figure is the reported post-rupture total attributed in the source to this line's outage.
global_pipelines.source: EIA Sudan/South Sudan Country Analysis Brief (Heglig-Port Sudan 450 kbd design); GEM Greater Nile (1,600 km, 250 kbd); Poten via Hellenic Shipping News (Bashayer 195 kbd Jan 2024 to 63 kbd Apr 2024)

global_pipelines.name: Petrodar Pipeline
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.28 x 500 kbd design capacity = 140 kbd. Basis for the low utilisation: South Sudan's Melut Basin (Blocks 3/7, Dar blend) output is a fraction of design capacity and the line was reportedly water-filled during the 2012-13 shutdown; no current reported throughput was found. Length 850 miles (~1,366 km) and 500 kbd design from EIA.
global_pipelines.source: EIA Sudan/South Sudan Country Analysis Brief (Petrodar ~850 mi, 500 kbd design, heated Dar blend line)

global_pipelines.name: ESPO — Taishet to Skovorodino (trunk)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED as the sum of its two measured/modelled downstream legs, to avoid inventing a trunk meter reading: Kozmino leg 859 kbd (measured, see Skovorodino-Kozmino line) + Daqing spur 600 kbd (modelled, see Skovorodino-Daqing line) = 1,459 kbd. System capacity 1,600 kbd is the Transneft expansion target reported by Wikipedia/GEM (initial 600, then 1,000, then 1,600 kbd).
global_pipelines.source: Derived — see the two downstream ESPO lines; Wikipedia/GEM ESPO (capacity path to 1,600 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: ESPO — Skovorodino to Kozmino
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (terminal loadings): Transneft reported Kozmino crude loadings of 42.8 Mt in 2023, up 9.4% (TASS via Hellenic Shipping News / Reuters) = ~859 kbd. Transneft guided 46 Mt for 2024 (~923 kbd) and Kozmino loadings ran near 1,000 kbd in mid-2024 months per Reuters trading sources, but the full-year reported outturn used here is 2023. Capacity: Kozmino port capacity was raised toward 50 Mtpa (~1,000 kbd).
global_pipelines.source: Transneft via TASS/Reuters Jan 2024 (Kozmino 42.8 Mt 2023); Reuters Jul/Sep 2024-25 monthly loading reports (~1,000 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: ESPO — Skovorodino to Daqing Spur (Russia–China Crude Oil Pipeline)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED by subtraction from a published total: Transneft reported direct pipeline supplies to China of 40 Mt in 2023, unchanged from 2022 (Reuters/Interfax). Of that, ~10 Mt/yr is the contracted Russian transit via Kazakhstan (Atasu, KazTransOil/Rosneft contract figure), leaving ~30 Mt/yr attributed to the Skovorodino-Daqing spur = ~600 kbd (30 Mt at 7.33 bbl/t / 365 = 602, rounded down to the line's 600 kbd nameplate). That attribution is an inference from two published figures, hence MODELLED. Spur capacity 600 kbd per Wikipedia (the China link), consistent with 30 Mtpa.
global_pipelines.source: Transneft via Reuters Jan 2024 (pipeline supplies to China 40 Mt 2023); KazTransOil Rosneft transit contract (10 Mt/yr via Kazakhstan); Wikipedia ESPO (China link 600 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: Kazakhstan–China Pipeline (Atasu–Alashankou)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (operator transshipment total): KazTransOil reported 11.190 Mt transshipped into the Atasu-Alashankou trunk in 2024, matching 2023 = ~225 kbd. Composition cross-check from KMG: ~10 Mt of that is Russian transit oil (Rosneft contract, 10 Mt/yr to 2033) and ~1.2 Mt is Kazakh export oil. Note KMG's wider Kazakhstan-China Pipeline LLP system total (18.789 Mt in 2024) includes domestic and Kenkiyak-Kumkol legs and is NOT this line's flow. Capacity 20 Mtpa = ~400 kbd.
global_pipelines.source: KazTransOil 2024 results (11.190 Mt into Atasu-Alashankou); KMG Annual Report midstream table; GEM Atasu-Alashankou (965 km, 20 Mtpa)

global_pipelines.name: Sino-Myanmar Crude Oil Pipeline
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.36 x capacity, rounded to 160 kbd. Capacity itself conflicts: design 22 Mtpa (~440 kbd) in CNPC/project sources vs Wikipedia's stated maximum discharge of 240 kbd and a 12 Mtpa figure in the same article. The Kunming (Anning) refinery it feeds is ~260 kbd (13 Mtpa), which bounds sustained flow. No reported annual throughput was found; the line has also been exposed to Myanmar's civil war since 2021. 160 kbd is a stated assumption below the refinery bound, not a measurement.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia/GEM Sino-Myanmar (771 km Myanmar section; capacity figures conflict 240-440 kbd); CNPC project descriptions (22 Mtpa design)

global_pipelines.name: Western Crude Oil Pipeline (Urumqi–Lanzhou), China
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: capacity 20 Mtpa (~400 kbd) for the Urumqi-Lanzhou western crude trunk; flow assumed at 0.7 x capacity = 280 kbd. No PipeChina/CNPC line-level throughput was found in open sources. This line carries Xinjiang crude plus Kazakhstan-China imports east from Urumqi to the Lanzhou hub.
global_pipelines.source: CNPC/PipeChina western pipeline descriptions (Urumqi-Lanzhou, ~1,858 km, 20 Mtpa); route via Turpan/Hami/Jiayuguan/Wuwei

global_pipelines.name: Alashankou–Dushanzi Pipeline, China
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED: flow set equal to the measured inflow at its origin — the Atasu-Alashankou line delivered 11.190 Mt in 2024 (KazTransOil, ~225 kbd) and this line is the continuation of that stream into the Dushanzi refinery/petrochemical complex, so its flow is modelled as the same volume, ignoring any Xinjiang field injections en route. Capacity was doubled to 20 Mtpa (~400 kbd) in 2013 (Xinhua via Platts reporting). Length is approximate.
global_pipelines.source: Modelled from KazTransOil Atasu-Alashankou 2024 inflow; Xinhua/Platts 2013 (Alashankou-Dushanzi expanded to 20 Mtpa)

global_pipelines.name: Lanzhou–Chengdu (Pengzhou) Pipeline, China
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.7 x capacity, rounded to 140 kbd. Capacity correction: GEM gives 200,684 b/d (10 Mtpa), corroborated by PetroChina's completion release ('10 million mt/year, 200,800 b/d'); Wikipedia's infobox figure of 20,080 b/d is a decimal error (it mis-converts 10 Mtpa) and is not used. No reported throughput found.
global_pipelines.source: GEM Lanzhou-Chengdu (880 km, 200,684 b/d / 10 Mtpa); PetroChina completion release 2013 via Platts

global_pipelines.name: Salaya–Mathura Pipeline (SMPL), India
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (filed, old vintage): Government of India pipeline-network table gives SMPL throughput of 23,135 thousand tonnes in FY2020-21 (25,492 kt in FY2019-20) = ~463 kbd on the FY2020-21 figure. No newer line-level throughput was found in IndianOil reporting (IndianOil reports network totals only). Capacity: IndianOil states 25 MMTPA installed for the 2,663 km system (which includes the Viramgam-Koyali branch and the Mathura-Panipat/Jalandhar extensions; the original Salaya-Mathura section is ~1,256 km — the length conflict is noted, and the operator's current system length is carried).
global_pipelines.source: IndianOil crude pipelines page (2,663 km, 25 MMTPA); Govt of India Updated Pipeline Network table (SMPL throughput 23,135 kt FY2020-21)

global_pipelines.name: Mundra–Panipat Pipeline (MPPL), India
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (filed, old vintage): Government of India pipeline table gives MPPL throughput of 6,093 thousand tonnes in FY2020-21 (6,826 kt in FY2019-20) = ~122 kbd. Capacity: IndianOil 8.4 MMTPA (~168 kbd) for the 1,194 km line; GEM notes an augmentation from 6 to 9 MMTPA was completed in 2011, a minor conflict with the current 8.4 MMTPA operator figure, which is carried.
global_pipelines.source: IndianOil crude pipelines page (1,194 km, 8.4 MMTPA); Govt of India Updated Pipeline Network table (MPPL throughput 6,093 kt FY2020-21); GEM Mundra-Panipat

global_pipelines.name: Paradip–Haldia–Barauni Pipeline (PHBPL), India
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED (filed, old vintage): Government of India pipeline table gives PHBPL throughput of 14,902 thousand tonnes in FY2020-21 (15,113 kt in FY2019-20) = ~299 kbd, on a 15.2 MMTPA capacity figure in that table. Conflict: IndianOil's current page states 20.4 MMTPA installed capacity and 1,465 km for the system (the government table lists 1,355 km); the operator's current capacity (20.4 MMTPA = ~408 kbd) is carried, with the throughput measured against the older capacity implying ~98% utilisation in FY2020-21 — high but consistent with the filed numbers.
global_pipelines.source: IndianOil crude pipelines page (1,465 km, 20.4 MMTPA); Govt of India Updated Pipeline Network table (PHBPL throughput 14,902 kt FY2020-21, 15.2 MMTPA in that table)

global_pipelines.name: SOTE (Trans-Ecuadorian Pipeline)
global_pipelines.flow_note: MEASURED: EP Petroecuador reported SOTE transported 104,348,303 bbl of Oriente crude in 2024 (Energy Analytics Institute, 20 Jan 2025, citing Petroecuador) = 104.35 Mbbl / 365 = ~286 kbd, at 90.9% of its annual operating-plan target. Capacity 360 kbd (Petroecuador/Rystad). Status: SOTE was shut by erosion/landslide force majeure in Jul 2025 and has had repeated Coca River erosion outages, so the 2024 average is not a current rate.
global_pipelines.source: EP Petroecuador via Energy Analytics Institute (104.35 Mbbl in 2024); Rystad/OilPrice (SOTE capacity 360 kbd, Jul 2025 shutdown)

global_pipelines.name: OCP (Oleoducto de Crudos Pesados), Ecuador
global_pipelines.flow_note: MODELLED from a published split: Rystad, citing official data, reported SOTE + OCP together transported an average 460 kbd in Jan-May 2025, with SOTE 57% and OCP 43% — 0.43 x 460 = ~198 kbd for OCP. That is a derived share of a reported total, hence MODELLED. Both lines were near-zero in mid-Jul 2025 during the erosion shutdown (OCP ~3.5 kbd on 13 Jul 2025), so this is a pre-shutdown 2025 rate, not a current one.
global_pipelines.source: Rystad Energy Jul 2025 (combined 460 kbd Jan-May 2025, OCP 43%); GEM OCP (485 km, 450 kbd)

global_pipelines.name: Ocensa Pipeline, Colombia
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.6 x 615 kbd = 370 kbd. The 0.6 utilisation is chosen because Colombian ministry material states the country's main pipelines 'work at 60% of their operational capacity' due to field decline — a published system-level utilisation, applied here as a stated assumption rather than a line measurement. Capacity 615 kbd and the La Belleza-Vasconia-Covenas length of 790 km are from the same ministry source; total Cusiana-Covenas routing is ~830 km.
global_pipelines.source: Republic of Colombia Ministry of Mines & Energy petroleum-chain study (Ocensa 615 kbd, 790 km Vasconia-Covenas, main lines at ~60% utilisation)

global_pipelines.name: Cano Limon–Covenas Pipeline, Colombia
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow set at 100 kbd, the 'normally transports about 100,000 b/d' figure given in Oil & Gas Journal's reporting on the line — an old, unattributed normal-rate figure rather than a dated measurement, so it is labelled ASSUMED, not measured. Capacity conflicts: 210 / 220 / 225 / 240 kbd across sources; 225 (Wikipedia maximum discharge) is carried. The line is attacked so frequently (26 explosive attacks Jan-Aug 2025 per Ecopetrol via Reuters) that any annual average is unstable.
global_pipelines.source: Wikipedia Cano Limon-Covenas (780 km, 225 kbd); OGJ (normally ~100 kbd, 240 kbd capacity in that account); Reuters 2025 (attack frequency)

global_pipelines.name: OSPAR Pipeline, Brazil
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.7 x capacity, rounded to 120 kbd. Capacity 8.52 Mtpa (~171 kbd) and length 117 km from GEM/Transpetro data for this crude line from the Sao Francisco do Sul (TEFRAN) terminal to the REPAR refinery. No reported throughput found. Included as Brazil's clearest crude trunk; most other Brazilian 'oleodutos' are products lines.
global_pipelines.source: GEM OSPAR (117 km, 8.52 Mtpa, 30-inch, operating since 1976); Transpetro/Petrobras

global_pipelines.name: OSBRA Pipeline, Brazil (products — not crude)
global_pipelines.flow_note: ASSUMED: flow = 0.7 x capacity, rounded to 72 kbd. Capacity is 6,000,000 m3/year of products (GEM/Transpetro) = ~103 kbd of product volume. IMPORTANT SCOPE NOTE: OSBRA carries diesel, gasoline, jet fuel and LPG, not crude oil — it is included only because the task scope named it ('OSBRA / ORBIG as fits'), and it should be dropped or re-styled if the globe layer is crude-only. No reported throughput found.
global_pipelines.source: GEM OSBRA (964 km, 6 Mm3/yr, products, operating since 1996); Transpetro/Petrobras

This is the 'TMX step-up, Jan 2027' carried in the outlook (nameplate 890 -> 980; it is a DRA step toward the demonstrated system, not the MOP). The maintenance forecast 2026-10-26 confirms 'early January 2027' and corrects an earlier Q4 2026 timing.

assumptions.assumption_note: Enbridge Mainline Optimization Phase 1 (MLO1) in service
assumptions.basis: Enbridge FID Nov 14, 2025, US$1.4B, +150 kb/d sanctioned (level verified). TIMING CONFLICT (kept open): the 2026-09-30 scrub found the schedule coded Jan 2027 while a Jul 2026 Enbridge disclosure says in service END-2027; the live builder codes Sep 2027 (house ruling 2026-10-01: Enbridge guides 'in-service by 2027', Jan deemed too aggressive). 2027 annual average in the live builder is therefore 3250, not 3350. Do not present the month as settled.

assumptions.assumption_note: Express +30 kb/d via Southern Illinois Connector
assumptions.basis: Enbridge Q3 2025 FID (level sanctioned). TIMING CONFLICT resolved in the live builder toward 2028: the scrub (2026-09-30) flagged sources split 2026 vs 2028 and the builder then assumed Jan 2026; the current live builder defers the step to Jan 2028 (310 flat through 2027).

supply.name: Eagle Ford condensate (Texas)
supply.basis: NOT PINNED — EIA's current public STEO/DPR series report the Eagle Ford region as crude oil + lease condensate COMBINED (1.12 MMb/d avg 2025, 1.10 MMb/d 2026E, EIA STEO Sep 2025); no current public EIA series splits lease condensate out for the play. Older (2014-15) condensate-heavy character is documented but not a current number

supply.name: Qatar — North Field (North Dome) condensate
supply.basis: MEASURED — Global Energy Monitor tracker: North Field condensate production 226.22 million bbl in 2022 = ~620 kb/d. Cross-checks: QatarEnergy North Field East expansion adds ~260 kb/d of condensate on top of the existing base (QatarEnergy project disclosures, 2022); Qatar condensate exports ran ~500 kb/d before the Laffan 2 splitter start (2016)
supply.source: Global Energy Monitor, North Field Oil and Gas Project (production table, data year 2022); QatarEnergy NFE disclosures

supply.name: Iran — South Pars condensate
supply.basis: MEASURED (official statement) — South Pars Gas Complex CEO: 780 kb/d of gas condensate from the South Pars refineries (IRNA via Iran Daily). CONFLICT: SPGC Site-2 deputy said 'over 710 kb/d' in Feb 2025 (ANA/IRNA); EIA (via Reuters/Bousso, Jun 2025) puts ALL-Iran condensate at ~1.3 MMb/d in 2025, of which South Pars is the dominant share (~700 kb/d per the same reporting). Pin carries the 780 official figure; treat the honest range as 710-780
supply.source: South Pars Gas Complex CEO via IRNA / Iran Daily; ANA Feb 2025; EIA via Reuters Jun 2025

demand.name: Yeosu petrochemical complex — condensate/naphtha-range feed demand (PROXY)
demand.basis: PROXY, not condensate capacity: Yeosu is South Korea's largest petrochemical complex with ethylene capacity above 6 Mtpa (Yeochun NCC 2.29 + LG Chem 2.08 + Lotte Chemical 1.23 + GS Caltex 0.90 Mtpa, per 2026 restructuring reporting). Its crackers run on naphtha, much of it made from imported condensate in Korean splitters. No public condensate-feed-only capacity exists; ethylene Mtpa is the stated proxy. Note: a government-backed restructuring will idle ~1.39 Mtpa of Yeosu ethylene capacity over ~3 years (approved Jul 2026 reporting)
demand.source: Korean petrochemical restructuring reporting (Cashfeed/Yuanta, 2026; ChemOrbis, Sep 2026)

demand.name: Daesan petrochemical complex — cracker feed demand (PROXY)
demand.basis: PROXY: Daesan crackers include Lotte Chemical's 1.1 Mtpa naphtha cracker — taken offline 1 Sep 2026 and shut indefinitely under the Korean restructuring (ChemOrbis) — plus HD Hyundai Chemical / Hanwha units beside the Daesan splitters (separate pins). Ethylene capacity is the proxy; condensate enters via the co-located splitters' naphtha output
demand.source: Reuters (Mar 2020) for the 1.1 Mtpa Lotte Daesan cracker; ChemOrbis (Sep 2026) for the shutdown

demand.name: Edmonton / Fort Saskatchewan blending hub — DILUENT DEMAND (basin)

Demand = blend requirement on the bitumen + conventional-heavy pools at CORE blend rates (solver test S-1 identity). This pin carries the BASIN total; Edmonton/Fort Saskatchewan is the hub pin, Hardisty (next pin) is inside the same number, not additive

The committed-class split is unpublished (classes are filed, the split is not); 60 is the stack's standing convention, re-run at 0/60/110 in solver_sensitivity.csv — the split moves no shortfall answer. Spot clears on top of base up to the 110 total when the residual calls for it

damage.site: Kharg Island — military targets (oil infrastructure deliberately spared)
damage.what_was_hit: More than 90 Iranian military targets: naval mine storage facilities, missile storage bunkers and other military sites. CENTCOM stated explicitly the strike was executed 'while preserving the oil infrastructure.' This pin corrects the common misreading that Kharg's oil terminal was destroyed in March.
damage.return_reporting: Oil infrastructure was not hit, so there was no oil outage to return from. NIOC chief Hamid Bovard said on 2026-09-02 (Reuters) that conditions on Kharg were 'calm and appropriate' and production/operations continued, rejecting a later claim that the terminal had been destroyed (see UNCONFIRMED list: the 2026-08-30 video was assessed by Reuters as most likely AI-generated). Kharg's export *flow* is governed by the Hormuz transit episode, not by terminal damage.

damage.site: Ras Tanura refinery and export complex
damage.what_was_hit: Two drones intercepted over the complex; debris caused a limited fire (Saudi defence ministry via SPA/Al Arabiya, reported by Reuters). Aramco shut the refinery as a precaution while damage was assessed. Satellite imagery reported by other outlets suggested a larger fire at processing units — that reading conflicts with the official 'limited' account and is NOT adopted here (see notes).
damage.return_reporting: Saudi energy ministry official via SPA (Reuters, 2026-03-03): supply of petroleum and derivatives to local markets was not affected; the situation was 'under control.' No tier-1 statement of a prolonged outage was found. A separate, later claim of a Houthi strike on Ras Tanura on 2026-10-18 was found only in non-tier-1 outlets and is listed as UNCONFIRMED, not as a new event on this pin.

damage.what_was_hit: A drone fell on the refinery on 2026-03-19; Saudi defence ministry said damage was being assessed. Yanbu is the Red Sea outlet for Saudi crude bypassing Hormuz via the East-West pipeline, so the hit targeted the bypass route itself.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return-to-service statement was found in this scour beyond the 2026-03-19 damage-assessment statement. Status is therefore 'partial / return not tier-1 verified' rather than an assumed full return.

damage.what_was_hit: Reported targeted later in the episode while already out of service. Tier-1 detail on the specific strike date and unit damage is thin; included because multiple round-ups of Reuters/IEA reporting list it among hit Saudi plants, with the 'already out of service' qualifier preserved.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 statement of a completed return was found. A non-tier-1 account claims a 2026-07-27 shutdown after its power plant and tank farm were hit and disrupted restarts in August–September; that detail is flagged in the notes as not tier-1 verified and is not loaded into the status beyond 'offline, return unverified.'

sources.outlet: Reuters/IEA reporting as summarised in market round-ups

damage.what_was_hit: A drone hit an operational unit, causing a fire; no injuries reported (Kuwait state news agency KUNA, reported by Reuters 2026-03-19). An earlier 2026-03-02 incident involved falling debris from intercepted missiles.
damage.return_reporting: KUNA reported the fire; no tier-1 statement quantifying lost capacity or a full return date was found. Capacity shown is the plant's nameplate, not a measured loss — Reuters did not report the plant as fully offline.

damage.what_was_hit: An operational unit was targeted by drones, resulting in a fire (KUNA, reported by Reuters 2026-03-19).
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 statement quantifying the outage or confirming a full return was found; do not read nameplate as lost output.

damage.site: Fujairah port and oil industry zone (ADNOC crude terminal / SPMs)
damage.what_was_hit: Drone attack and debris from interceptions sparked fires in the petroleum industrial zone (Fujairah government media office). ADNOC suspended crude loading; two of three single-point moorings were reported operational while ADNOC crude loading remained halted (Reuters sources, 2026-03-16). Fujairah is the Hormuz bypass outlet for about 1,000 kb/d of Murban crude and exported about 1,700 kb/d of crude and fuels in 2025 (Kpler via Reuters).
damage.return_reporting: Reuters (2026-03-16): some loading at the hub had restarted and two of three SPMs were operational, while ADNOC crude loading was still halted at that time. This was the second disruption in days; operations had resumed on 2026-03-15 after the weekend strike before being suspended again.

damage.site: Ras Laffan Industrial City — Pearl GTL and LNG facilities (QatarEnergy)
damage.what_was_hit: Missile attacks on 2026-03-18 extensively damaged the Pearl GTL facility; further missile attacks in the early hours of 2026-03-19 hit several LNG facilities, causing sizeable fires and 'extensive further damage' (QatarEnergy official statement). QatarEnergy CEO Saad al-Kaabi told Reuters the strikes knocked out 17% of Qatar's LNG export capacity, with force majeure on some long-term contracts possible for up to five years.
damage.return_reporting: QatarEnergy (2026-03-19): all fires brought under control, no casualties. No tier-1 return-to-full-capacity statement was found; the CEO's five-year force-majeure warning is the governing return reporting. Capacity is LNG/GTL, so capacity_affected is left null in oil kb/d terms rather than converted.

damage.site: Habshan gas facilities and Bab oil field
damage.what_was_hit: Falling debris from intercepted missiles forced a shutdown of the Habshan gas processing facilities and hit the Bab oil field (UAE authorities, reported by Reuters 2026-03-19).
damage.return_reporting: Reuters reported the shutdown; no tier-1 restart statement was found in this scour. Gas processing, so no oil kb/d figure is assigned.

damage.what_was_hit: Attack on the Bapco oil refinery on Sitra Island on 2026-03-09; Reuters published photographs of smoke rising following the attack. Unit-level damage was not specified in tier-1 reporting retrieved.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 statement on outage size or return was found; nameplate shown, loss not measured.

damage.site: South Pars / Asaluyeh gas processing complex
damage.what_was_hit: Israeli strikes on South Pars gas facilities on 2026-03-18 — the event Tehran cited when it retaliated against Gulf energy sites the same day (Reuters). Secondary reporting describes four gas processing units offline at Asaluyeh; that unit count is not in the Reuters copy retrieved and is recorded here as secondary, not tier-1.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 Iranian return statement was found. NIORDC's general statement that fuel supply remained stable is an official Iranian claim recorded in secondary reporting, not a facility-level return confirmation.

damage.what_was_hit: Drone attacks shut the East-West pipeline itself in mid-September 2026. The line had been carrying about 4,000 kb/d to Yanbu, the kingdom's main Hormuz bypass.
damage.return_reporting: Reuters (2026-09-22, sources briefed on the matter): Saudi Arabia restarted the pipeline, initially at a low rate; a security source told Reuters a full resumption could take weeks. Status 'returned' means restarted, not back to the pre-shutdown rate.

damage.what_was_hit: Repeated drone attacks on tankers and loading equipment at the CPC terminal through 2026. CPC itself said two tankers (ASIA and NISSOS IOS) were attacked during loading, one caught fire (extinguished), no injuries and no oil spill, and loadings were suspended (CPC statement via Reuters, July 2026). A further drone incident on 2026-09-08 briefly halted loading; Kazakhstan's Energy Ministry said inspections found no damage affecting continued loading and loading resumed with no CPC restrictions on accepting Kazakh crude.
damage.return_reporting: Kazakhstan Energy Ministry (via reporting of its statement, 2026-09-10): loading resumed after the September incident. July's suspension forced Kazakhstan to cut production because terminal storage filled (Kazakh energy ministry statement via Reuters, 2026-07-23). An April attack's specific damage claims (SPM/berth/tanks, '65% capacity') come from non-tier-1 trackers and are NOT adopted — see UNCONFIRMED list.

damage.what_was_hit: Ukrainian drone strikes; Reuters reported on 2026-09-15 that Kirishi — one of Russia's six largest diesel plants, together about half of national diesel output — had shut completely after strikes that month.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return statement was found after 2026-09-15. The tasking line 'offline since Sep 29' was NOT verified in tier-1 reporting retrieved: the dated tier-1 anchor is the Reuters 2026-09-15 report of a complete shutdown. A secondary log notes Kirishi's current status 'has not been verified' — that uncertainty is preserved here.

damage.what_was_hit: Repeated drone attacks. Most recently, a large drone attack on 2026-10-15 caused a fire at the refinery (Ryazan governor Pavel Malkov, reported by Reuters the same day); Reuters separately reported the CDU-6 primary unit shut after the 2026-10-15 strike while three other primary units operated. Bloomberg's Rosneft tally (2026-10-22) says Ryazan was idle more than half the time after its first attack in May 2026 and ran heavily underloaded.
damage.return_reporting: Reuters (2026-10-16): three of four primary units operating, CDU-6 shut — i.e. partial operation, not a full return. Governor Malkov on 2026-10-15 said material damage was still being assessed.

damage.what_was_hit: Drone attacks on 2026-05-29, 2026-07-31 and 2026-10-02 (Reuters). After the October attack Reuters reported, citing sources, that the plant stopped ALL crude processing (2026-10-06). In September it had already been running at about a quarter of nameplate (Reuters, 2026-09-15).
damage.return_reporting: Reuters (2026-10-06) is the latest tier-1 status: all crude processing stopped. No later tier-1 return statement was found.

damage.site: NORSI refinery, Kstovo (Lukoil, Nizhny Novgorod region)
damage.what_was_hit: Drone strikes; Reuters reported on 2026-09-15 that NORSI was running at about a quarter of nameplate capacity after strikes.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return-to-normal statement was found after 2026-09-15.

damage.what_was_hit: Repeated drone strikes; Bloomberg's tally of confirmed strikes (2026-10-22) records Tuapse as non-operational since April 2026 and among the three hardest-hit Rosneft plants (with Ryazan and Syzran).
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return statement was found; Bloomberg's October tally still lists it non-operational. Event date is given as April 2026 (month precision only in the source).

damage.what_was_hit: Repeated drone strikes; Bloomberg (2026-10-22) records Syzran as idle or running below a third of capacity for most of the six months to October. September round-ups also list a Syzran stoppage among Rosneft disruptions.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return statement was found. Event date is the date of the Bloomberg status tally, not a single strike date.

damage.what_was_hit: Drone-related fire; September reporting summarising Reuters listed a halt in crude processing at Gazprom Neft's Moscow refinery after drone-related fires, and a mid-September strike on this plant is the event behind Ukraine's (unverified) claim of 45%+ of national capacity disabled.
damage.return_reporting: No tier-1 return statement was found. Ukraine's 45% capacity claim is NOT adopted (see UNCONFIRMED list).

hotspots.name: Strait of Hormuz

last_change.what: Reuters analysis: Hormuz transit rose to about 82% of pre-war in October (11,700 kb/d, up from 9,750 kb/d in September), moving largely in US-Navy-escorted convoys along the Omani coast and via an Iranian-controlled northern route (about a third of transits), while tanker attacks continued — 12 reported in the week to mid-October (UKMTO) and the highest weekly attack total of the war in the week of Sep 28–Oct 5 (JMIC via Reuters).

hotspots.status_card: Oil is moving through Hormuz again at roughly four-fifths of its pre-war rate, but it moves dark, at night, in escorted convoys or on an Iranian-controlled northern route, and tankers are still being attacked. Volume has largely recovered; normal shipping has not. Vessel-count drops (UKMTO transits about 70% below pre-war in the week to Oct 14) count ships, not barrels, and are not used as a flow measure here.
hotspots.basis: Oil actually transiting the strait, October 2026 average (Kpler via Reuters analysis, 2026-10-22), equal to about 82% of the pre-war transit level. Pre-war reference: 20,700 kb/d total oil flow in 2024 (EIA, updated 2026-03-03), of which crude/condensate transit is the comparable subset. Total Middle East crude exports (all routes, incl. bypasses and Gulf-of-Oman ship-to-ship) averaged 17,300 kb/d in October vs 16,900 kb/d pre-war (Kpler via Reuters) — exports recovering is NOT the same as the strait normalising.

hotspots.name: Bab el-Mandeb / Red Sea

last_change.what: UKMTO reported an attempted attack on a tanker south of Al Mukha (Mocha), Yemen — multiple explosions near the vessel, crew safe, no environmental impact; the Houthis did not claim it. IMO's record added no new confirmed Bab el-Mandeb merchant attack for Sep 28–Oct 4. Separately, fighting over the strait's shoreline in September–October (Houthi advance, then a Saudi-backed government counteroffensive retaking Perim/Mayyun per local reports via Reuters) is reported as contested, not settled.
last_change.source: UKMTO via SeaNews/Marine reporting, 2026-10-04; Reuters via reports, 2026-10-05

hotspots.status_card: The strait is not formally closed and most transits still use the established traffic lane, but Red Sea traffic runs roughly 60% below its pre-2023 level, war-risk terms apply, and the Yanbu bypass barrels Saudi Arabia sends around Hormuz must exit through this same threatened gate. An attack attempt in early October keeps the state at EPISODE even though confirmed hits have thinned.
hotspots.basis: EIA 1H25 oil flow through Bab el-Mandeb (4,100 kb/d in 2024), down from 9,300 kb/d in 2023 before the Houthi campaign.

hotspots.name: Strait of Malacca

last_change.what: No tier-1 reported disruption. The last tier-1 state-relevant event is the EIA chokepoint update itself; Malacca's strain is indirect — it carries the Asian demand that Hormuz bypasses and reroutes still have to reach.

hotspots.status_card: Malacca is operating normally and no tier-1 source reports an incident there. Its importance in this episode is as the destination lane: crude that escapes the Gulf by bypass pipeline, ship-to-ship transfer or the Cape route still largely funnels through Malacca to Northeast Asian refiners.
hotspots.basis: EIA 1H25 oil flow, the world's largest chokepoint volume (22,500 kb/d in 2024).

hotspots.name: Taiwan Strait

last_change.what: No tier-1 reported oil-flow disruption found in this scour. Scheduled or announced military exercises are not state changes under the house rule and none are recorded as one.

hotspots.status_card: No tier-1 source reports disrupted oil flow through the Taiwan Strait. The pin exists because a Taiwan contingency would strand Northeast Asian crude and LNG arrivals that have no short-notice substitute route at scale — it is a watch pin, not an episode pin.
hotspots.basis: No EIA oil-flow series exists for the Taiwan Strait as a standalone chokepoint; most Northeast Asia crude transits Malacca/South China Sea routes, with the Taiwan Strait one of two passages into the East China Sea. Assigning it a standalone kb/d would be inventing a number, so the value is null by design.

hotspots.name: Panama Canal

last_change.what: No tier-1 reported oil disruption; flows in EIA's latest table are above the drought-period level. The 2023–24 drought restriction episode is closed history, not the current state.

hotspots.status_card: The canal is transiting normally for oil and products traffic on the latest tier-1 data. It matters to this map mainly as a relief valve for US Gulf Coast exports to Asia when Pacific routing tightens, and that valve is open.
hotspots.basis: EIA 1H25 oil flow by fiscal year (2,000 kb/d in FY2024).

hotspots.name: Suez Canal / SUMED

last_change.what: Shipping lines had gradually resumed some Suez transits despite continuing security concerns (reporting to 2026-10-16), while the early-October Bab el-Mandeb attack attempt shows the southern approach remains threatened — partial recovery, not normalisation.
last_change.source: Marine/industry reporting of EU Aspides posture, 2026-10-16; UKMTO, 2026-10-04

hotspots.status_card: Suez oil flow is running at a little over half its 2023 level because many owners still route around the Cape, adding ten-plus days. Some carriers are coming back under naval escort, but the canal's state follows Bab el-Mandeb: as long as the southern gate is an episode, Suez stays strained.
hotspots.basis: EIA 1H25 combined Suez Canal + SUMED pipeline oil flow (4,800 kb/d in 2024), down from 8,800 kb/d in 2023 — the drop is the Red Sea diversion around the Cape of Good Hope, whose flow rose to 9,100–9,300 kb/d.

hotspots.name: Venezuela (crude production and exports)

last_change.what: OFAC issued General Licence 50C naming six companies authorised to work Venezuela's oil and gas sector (BP, Shell, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol), with royalties payable into a US Treasury-designated account and reporting to State/DOE every 90 days.

hotspots.status_card: Venezuelan oil now moves under a US-written licensing regime: foreign majors operate, but royalties route through a Treasury-designated account and activity is reported to Washington quarterly. Production continues; the strain is legal and financial, not physical, and a licence change in Washington is the event that moves this pin.
hotspots.basis: Origin volume, approximate: national crude production around 1,000 kb/d in 2026 reporting; Chevron's joint ventures alone exported about 150 kb/d under its restricted US licence (Reuters). Treated as an order-of-magnitude origin pin, not a measured export series.

hotspots.name: Libya (production and Zawiya export route)

last_change.what: Individuals entered the crude receiving station near Zawiya refinery and closed the pipeline valve from the Hamada and Tahara fields, cutting output at both fields (NOC statement; NOC chief to Reuters). In September an armed group had closed valve 7 on the Sharara–Zawiya pipeline, sharply reducing Sharara output.

hotspots.status_card: Libya is still producing about 1.4 million barrels a day, but single valves on the pipelines to Zawiya keep being closed by armed groups and protesters, and each closure shuts in the fields behind it. No force majeure had been declared on the October closure in the reporting retrieved — the pattern, not any one valve, is the strain.
hotspots.basis: National oil output 'remains at around 1,400 kb/d' — NOC/Reuters, 2026-10-22.

hotspots.name: Niger Delta (Nigeria crude production and exports)

last_change.what: No tier-1 reported Delta outage, force majeure or state-changing incident was found in this scour. Absence of a found incident is recorded as a scour result, not as proof nothing happened.

hotspots.status_card: No tier-1 source in this scour reports a new Niger Delta disruption; the pin is carried at NORMAL with that limitation stated plainly. The standing risks — theft, pipeline vandalism and community shutdowns — are chronic background, and only a dated, sourced incident moves this state.
hotspots.basis: Origin volume, approximate: Nigerian crude production in the roughly 1,500 kb/d range in 2026 OPEC secondary-source reporting. Order-of-magnitude pin only; no fresh tier-1 Delta-specific series was retrieved in this scour.

hotspots.name: Russia export ports — Baltic (Primorsk / Ust-Luga)

last_change.what: Diesel loadings resumed from Primorsk — a tanker loaded about 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low-sulphur diesel for Morocco (LSEG data via Reuters, 2026-10-14) — after OFAC GL 135 (2026-10-09) and Moscow's partial lifting of its diesel export ban (2026-10-10). The Baltic ports were also struck earlier in 2026 (fuel reservoir hit at Primorsk, Reuters, 2026-04-05).

hotspots.status_card: The Baltic is Russia's working export lung: crude loads, and diesel has started loading again under the October US licence and Russia's partial ban-lift. It stays strained because the ports sit within Ukrainian drone range, were hit in the spring, and every cargo still has to clear the sanctions and shadow-fleet thicket that the UK and EU added to in October.
hotspots.basis: Approximate seaborne crude loading capacity/volume of Russia's Baltic outlets; western-ports exports (Primorsk, Ust-Luga, Novorossiysk combined) were reported at 1,950–2,250 kb/d in late-2024 Reuters trade reporting. Baltic-only split is an approximation and is labelled as such; no current tier-1 Baltic-only series was retrieved.

hotspots.name: Russia export ports — Black Sea (Novorossiysk / Sheskharis + CPC)

last_change.what: A drone incident near the CPC terminal briefly halted loading (the latest in a run of July–September suspensions, including CPC's July suspension after two tankers were attacked during loading). Kazakhstan said loading resumed with no CPC intake restrictions after inspections.
last_change.source: CPC statement via Reuters, 2026-07-20; Kazakhstan Energy Ministry (reported), 2026-09-10

hotspots.status_card: Black Sea loadings at Novorossiysk have stopped and restarted repeatedly since July as tankers and terminal equipment are attacked; in July the stoppage filled terminal storage and forced Kazakhstan to cut production. Baltic and Black Sea are pinned separately because they fail differently: the Baltic's problem is sanctions and drone range, the Black Sea's is live attacks on the loading operation itself.
hotspots.basis: CPC pipeline nameplate/throughput of about 1,400 kb/d of mostly Kazakh crude to the Novorossiysk terminal (CPC/Reuters), plus Russian Sheskharis loadings at the same port complex (not quantified separately here to avoid double counting).

hotspots.name: Ecuador — OTE pipeline and Esmeraldas export route

last_change.what: No tier-1 reported OTE rupture, force majeure or export halt was found in this scour. Ecuador's history of landslide ruptures is background, not a current state.

hotspots.status_card: No tier-1 source in this scour reports the OTE line down. The pin is carried because a single landslide-prone pipeline carries most of Ecuador's exports and past ruptures have declared force majeure within days — a dated Petroecuador or Reuters report is what would move it.
hotspots.basis: OTE (Oleoducto Transecuatoriano) transport capacity of about 360 kb/d, the main route from Amazon fields to the Esmeraldas Pacific terminal; Ecuador's total production runs higher (about 480 kb/d) with the remainder on the OCP line.

hotspots.name: Iraq Kurdistan export route (Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline)

last_change.what: Crude flowed through the Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline for the first time in two and a half years after a Baghdad–KRG–producers deal (Iraq oil ministry, via Reuters). The line had been shut since March 2023 by the ICC arbitration ruling against Turkey.

hotspots.status_card: Kurdish crude is flowing to Ceyhan again at roughly 185,000 barrels a day under Baghdad's marketing control — a real recovery from a two-and-a-half-year shut-in. It stays strained because the deal is interim, the revenue and debt arguments that closed the line are not finally settled, and the route's northern-Iraq leg also depends on the same export system the Hormuz episode has stressed.
hotspots.basis: Exports of 180,000–190,000 kb/d scheduled at restart (Iraq oil minister via Rudaw, reported by Reuters, 2025-09-26), under a deal committing at least 230,000 kb/d of deliveries to SOMO with 50,000 kb/d kept for local use.

policy.decision: 2026 crude oil import quota for non-state (independent) refiners set at 257 million tonnes, unchanged from 2025 — about 5,140 kb/d equivalent across roughly 40 independent refiners. Allocations were released in batches through end-2025, with traders estimating about 70% of annual allowances issued including the first smaller batch.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: 257 Mt/yr converted at about 7.3 bbl/tonne over 365 days; quota ceiling for non-state traders only — state majors do not need import quotas, so this is not China's total import volume.

policy.decision: Crude import quotas issued for 2026 to three ex-Sinochem Shandong refineries now run by independent operators (Changyi Petrochemical, Zhenghe Group, Huaxing Petrochemical), totalling about 12 million tonnes (about 240 kb/d), letting the new owners buy crude directly instead of via Sinochem. Reuters sources said it was not immediately clear whether these were full annual amounts or partial shares.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: 12 Mt/yr as reported by Reuters trading sources.

policy.deciding_body: OPEC+ (seven core members: Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, Oman)
policy.decision: Production targets kept steady for November 2026 at a brief online meeting; no change to ceilings. The group noted members were pumping about 5,000 kb/d below pre-war February levels in August (25,000 kb/d) despite the targets, and delayed its capacity review for 2027 quotas because of the war. Next meeting set for 2026-11-01. Vienna is the OPEC secretariat pin; the decision was taken by the member group, not by Austria.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Actual August output of the seven core members (OPEC data via Reuters) — the volume the unchanged targets govern in practice; the paper targets are higher.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Total barrels authorised (400,000 bbl one-off), expressed in kb to match the field's unit convention — it is a stock exchange, not a daily rate.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Total barrels authorised (4.0 million bbl one-off), in kb per the field convention.

policy.decision: General License 135 issued, authorising transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel — including importation into the United States — through 12:01 a.m. EDT 2027-04-07. The licence does not authorise debits to US accounts of Russia's central bank, National Wealth Fund or finance ministry, and its fit with the statutory 2022 Russian-energy import ban was publicly disputed by lawyers and lawmakers (recorded, not resolved, here).

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: The licence text names no volumes. Announced supply tranches (300 kt in October, 500 kt in November, 1 Mt thereafter, per the President and Deputy PM Novak) are supply announcements, not licence volumes, and are not loaded as barrels touched.

The underlying Rosneft/Lukoil blocking sanctions date from 2025-10-22.
