policy.deciding_body: President of the United States (waiver under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, signed 2026-09-18)
policy.decision: Many of the Act's mandatory provisions were waived days before they were due to take effect (mid-October), including required sanctions on major Russian state banks and the shadow-fleet designation programme. Existing designations stayed in place; nothing new was added by the waiver.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Waiver of statutory sanctions provisions; no barrel volume is named. CREA estimated sanctioned shadow-fleet tankers carried 57% of Russia's seaborne oil in September 2026 — context for what the waived designation programme would have reached, not a licence volume.

source.outlet: Reporting of the waiver (Newsweek / sanctions analyses)

policy.deciding_body: US Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC)
policy.decision: General Licence 50C issued, naming six companies authorised to work Venezuela's oil and gas sector (BP, Shell, Chevron, Eni, Maurel & Prom, Repsol). Contracts with the Venezuelan government/PDVSA must specify dispute venues in the US, UK, France or Singapore; royalties are payable into a US Treasury-designated account; operators report to the State Department and DOE every 90 days.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Sector-wide authorisation; no volume is named in the licence. Chevron's roughly 150 kb/d of JV exports (Reuters) is the largest single-company flow under it.

policy.decision: Diesel export ban for producers extended through 2026-10-31 by government decree (2026-09-30), then partially lifted with effect 2026-10-10 following the Trump–Putin call, with contracted supplies to be approved by the government. Deputy PM Novak's announced schedule: 300 kt in October, 500 kt in November, 1 Mt in December, potentially returning to the usual 3.0–3.5 Mt/month by year-end. Remaining restrictions: gasoline exports and diesel exports by non-producers banned through 2027-01-31; jet-fuel export ban (in force since 2026-06-01) ends 2026-11-30.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Approximate: the usual diesel export rate of 3.0–3.5 Mt/month (Novak via Reuters) converts to roughly 730–860 kb/d at full restoration; the value shown is the mid-range of the announced Oct–Dec ramp (about 1.8 Mt over the quarter), stated as an approximation, not a decree figure.

policy.decision: 38 new Russia sanctions designations on 2026-10-08, including Russian oil companies and 12 additional shadow-fleet oil tankers, plus payment platforms and crypto exchanges; the UK states more than 600 shadow-fleet vessels have now been sanctioned or specified and the packages cover more than 90% of Russia's oil production capacity. A wind-down general licence for Zarubezhneft JSC transactions was issued the same day, expiring 2026-11-21. This followed 31 designations on 2026-10-01 targeting the LNG shadow fleet.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Designations list persons and vessels, not volumes; the 'more than 90% of production capacity' figure is the UK government's characterisation of cumulative coverage, recorded as such.

source.outlet: UK Government press release (via Mondaq/Fieldfisher sanctions updates)

policy.decision: EU designated 1,569 individuals and entities linked to Russia's military-industrial complex on 2026-10-12 — described as the single largest set of listings ever agreed by the EU, bringing total listings under the Russia regime to close to 4,600, with asset freezes and travel bans. The EU's 22nd sanctions package context includes the July 2026 vessel listings (41 vessels added to 632 already listed, with bunkering/support-service rules extended). Oil-flow relevance is via the military-industrial and shipping nexus; no crude volume is named.

barrels_touched_kbd.basis: Designation package; no barrel volume named.

floating_storage.method: Floating storage from the Narrows AIS archive (narrows.db, positions + vessels tables, read-only). Universe: vessels the archive types as tankers (AIS shiptype 80-89 in the vessels table; a full scan confirmed no additional tanker MMSIs exist in positions only). Each vessel's fixes are segmented into stays: a stay is anchored on its running centroid, a fix joins the stay when it lies within 1.0 km of that centroid (the anchor swing circle) and follows the stay's previous accepted fix by no more than 12 h; three consecutive fixes outside the circle close the stay (a real departure), while one or two outside fixes followed by a return inside are counted as position outliers of the stay. A stay is a floating-storage dwell when all of the following hold: (1) it is the vessel's trailing stay, ending at the vessel's last archive fix, and that fix is within 24 h of the archive's latest timestamp, so the vessel is still there at as_of; (2) its duration is at least 7.0 days; (3) stationary: at least 90% of its fixes report speed over ground < 0.5 kn; at least 95% of its fixes lie within 1.5 km of the stay centroid; the stay's first-day and last-day fix centroids lie within 1.5 km of each other (it ended where it began, so a slow-steaming transit cannot chain into a dwell); and the stay carries at least 100 accepted fixes (in-box vessels at anchor broadcast roughly 150 fixes a day, so the floor only kills phantom chains of sparse transit fixes). The speed test is applied to the stay as a whole, not fix by fix, because a vessel at anchor swings on its anchor and broadcasts occasional 0.5-0.6 kn readings without moving (a literal every-fix < 0.5 kn rule scores zero dwells anywhere in this archive, including a tanker that sat in one anchorage for two weeks broadcasting nav status 'at anchor' - that reading of the rule measures GPS swing, not movement, so position is treated as the ground truth of stationary and speed as corroboration); (4) not at a berth: neither the stay centroid nor any accepted fix falls inside a berth polygon the collector's event pipeline uses (Westridge berth; Cherry Point and Anacortes WA; Chevron Richmond, Marathon Martinez, Valero Benicia, Phillips 66 Rodeo, Long Beach and Chevron El Segundo CA; Montreal East and Levis St-Romuald on the St. Lawrence) - alongside a berth is a port call, not floating storage; (5) laden, by the draught call the globe stack computes (build_globe.py): median draught over the stay divided by the vessel's full-load draught from AIS static data, laden at ratio >= 0.85; where the archive holds no static draught for the vessel, the fallback call is median stay draught > 60% of the vessel's deepest draught observed anywhere in the archive, and laden_basis records which rule fired and the numbers behind it. lat/lon are the stay centroid (mean of its accepted fixes). est_cargo_bbl is null for every record: the archive holds no vessel size class, DWT or dimensions (the vessels table carries mmsi, IMO, name, shiptype, draught, destination and callsign only), so no cargo estimate is printed rather than inventing a size class; any future estimate from a size class will be labelled MODELLED. Stays that began before the archive's first fix are left-censored: their dwell_days are minimums and are flagged in the record.
floating_storage.coverage_note: The archive honestly covers only the three collector boxes the Narrows subscribes to at aisstream.io: (1) Pacific Northwest, 48.0-49.6 N, 125.0-122.4 W (Burrard Inlet and the Westridge berth, Strait of Georgia, Juan de Fuca approaches, Cherry Point and Anacortes WA); (2) California coast, 32.5-38.5 N, 123.0-121.0 W (San Francisco Bay refinery docks and anchorages, Long Beach, El Segundo); (3) St. Lawrence River, 45.30-47.10 N, 74.30-70.50 W (Montreal East, Trois-Rivieres gate, Levis). Archive window: 2026-10-03T16:34:54.375363+00:00 to 2026-10-27T04:50:44.573121+00:00 UTC (23.5 days), so a 7-day dwell is computable but nothing longer than the window can be seen, and any anchorage outside these three boxes is invisible. This is NOT global floating storage: the world's main floating-storage anchorages (off Singapore, Fujairah, Rotterdam, the US Gulf, West Africa and elsewhere) are outside the watched boxes. Global floating storage awaits the widened AIS net now being built; until it lands, this layer shows floating storage inside the watched boxes only.

cameras.view: Wide view from the North Vancouver side over Vancouver Harbour and Canada Place. ride.title: The Barrel Ride: one heavy barrel from a SAGD pad to a refinery in China
ride.label: REWIND: this ride is replayed from the archive, not live. Every position, price and event in it is dated October 2026.

date_window.detail: Tanker leg: SEAWAYS REYES arrived at Westridge on Oct 19, 2026, loaded for two days, sailed Oct 21, and was tracked to the edge of watched water on Oct 22. The barrel itself was produced in October 2026 (the model's October production month). The delivery leg after Oct 22 is labelled MODELLED wherever it appears: the archive holds no positions for it.
date_window.timezone_note: Event times are UTC as the archive records them, with Edmonton time (MDT, UTC-6) alongside.

barrel.grade: Diluted bitumen (dilbit) from SAGD, sold into the Western Canadian Select (WCS) heavy pool
barrel.origin_site: Christina Lake SAGD (Cenovus Energy), near Conklin, Alberta
barrel.destination_broadcast: Yangpu, Hainan, China (AIS destination field: CAVAN>CNYPG)

vessel.name: SEAWAYS REYES
vessel.ship_type_label: tanker (Aframax class; the Baltic TD28 route this cargo prices on is an 80,000 tonne Aframax route)

track_summary.extent_note: The track ends at longitude -124.989, eleven thousandths of a degree inside the western edge of the collector's Pacific Northwest watch box (which ends at -125.0). That is where the archive honestly ends: the separate global tanker collector held no positions yet at build time, so no offshore Pacific positions exist in the stack for this vessel.

hops.name: Origin: Christina Lake SAGD
hops.basis: ACTUAL (modelled production from the stack's own AER ST3 plant-grain balance; the site and its coordinates are the stack's own network nodes)
hops.arrive_note: The ride starts at a steam-assisted gravity drainage (SAGD) project in the Cold Lake oil sands country, where bitumen too thick to flow is steamed out of the ground and blended with diluent so it can move in a pipe as dilbit.
facts: Christina Lake is a SAGD project run by Cenovus Energy Inc. near Conklin, Alberta (operator and project type: the stack's project register, annotations/projects.yaml).

The stack's own production model puts Christina Lake at 205.8 thousand barrels a day in August 2026, the latest actuals month in the AER ST3 plant-grain file (site/api/st3.json, built Oct 26, 2026), and at 179.0 thousand barrels a day for October 2026, the month this barrel was produced. The October figure is a forecast; the August figure is the model's read of reported actuals.

Christina Lake is one site inside a very large in-situ system: total in-situ bitumen production is modelled at 2,057.7 thousand barrels a day for October 2026, of which SAGD is 1,443.7 thousand barrels a day (AER ST3 plant-grain file, October 2026 forecast).

The barrel's grade is diluted bitumen: non-upgraded bitumen supply for all of Alberta is modelled at 2,289.4 thousand barrels a day for October 2026 (AER ST3 plant-grain file). Dilbit from Christina Lake is sold into the Western Canadian Select heavy pool.

Why this site: it is a named SAGD project whose production the stack models plant by plant, and it has a plotted node and a named pipeline in the stack's own network files. A specific battery's modelled output is not held in the stack (the Petrinex material is used for validation, not per-battery modelling), so the ride starts at plant grain, which is the finest grain the stack honestly holds.

The arb at this hop: a December 2026 barrel of WCS at Hardisty settled at US$27.95 under WTI on Oct 20, 2026, on a traded print of 569 lots (ICE TMW December 2026 settle, the stack's ICE settlements file for Oct 20, 2026). That discount is the price of being heavy, sour and landlocked, and it is what the rest of this ride spends money to escape.

hops.name: Gathering: Access Pipeline to Edmonton
hops.basis: ACTUAL geometry from the stack's network file (its own source note calls the corridor waypoint approximate); toll state stated honestly
hops.arrive_note: The barrel leaves the plant diluted and rides the Access Pipeline southwest to the Edmonton area, the hub where Alberta barrels are stored, blended and handed to the big trunk lines.
facts: The gathering leg is the Access Pipeline from Christina Lake to the Edmonton area. Its geometry here is the stack's own: builders/site/map_data/c5_network.json draws the Access edge from the Christina Lake node (55.6, -110.9) through a corridor waypoint at (54.35, -112.1) to Edmonton / Fort Saskatchewan (53.63, -113.35), and its source note says the corridor waypoint is approximate.

The Access Pipeline also explains the diluent in the barrel: the same northeast Alberta corridor carries diluent north to the oil sands (the stack's c5 network draws the Polaris, Norlite and Corridor diluent legs on this corridor). Alberta's diluent imports are modelled at 310.2 thousand barrels a day for October 2026 (AER ST3 plant-grain file).

The tolls paid at this hop: none that the stack can print. The filed-tariff database (pipelines/tolls.db, 13 pipelines) holds no Access Pipeline tariff, so no gathering toll is quoted for this leg. The only filed toll on this whole ride is the Trans Mountain toll at the trunk hop. Anything else would be a guess, and the ride does not guess.
The arb at this hop: gathering is a cost the stack cannot price from a filed tariff, so it is carried as an unpriced leg in the closing arb. The priced stack starts at Edmonton.

hops.name: The hub: Edmonton and Hardisty storage
hops.basis: ACTUAL (AER ST3 closing stocks at their latest actuals month; the October balance line is the model's forecast and is labelled as such)
hops.arrive_note: At Edmonton the barrel joins the largest pool of stored crude in Western Canada. Whether storage is building or drawing decides how much room the system has before price has to do the work.
facts: Alberta crude inventories closed August 2026 at 60.04 million barrels, up 1.32 million barrels from July 2026. That is AER ST3 closing stocks, actuals through August 2026: the latest actuals month the model balance prints, carried in the globe's storage layer from hidden_files/woodmack_storage/st3_dashboard.json.

The model's own balance for October 2026, the ride's month, carries Alberta inventory at 58,720 thousand barrels with 21,896 thousand barrels of ullage (empty storage room) left. That line is a forecast, labelled model output in the balance file (site/api/balance.json, October 2026).

Hardisty, the heavy hub 200 kilometres southeast at 52.667, -111.302, has its own gauge the stack reads directly: the salt cavern brine pond. Oil pushed into the cavern pushes brine out to the pond, so the pond's water area is the cavern's surface gauge. Our Sentinel-1 reader measured 6,800 square metres of pond water on Oct 19, 2026, the day this ride's tanker arrived at Westridge (the globe's storage layer, from the Tank Watch pond reads). The area prints as an area, with no barrel conversion: the barrel conversion was calibrated against a licensed vendor print and is never published.

The arb at this hop: storage was not the problem in the ride's month. The October balance shows pipe exports of 4,179.9 thousand barrels a day against 4,411.4 thousand barrels a day of Alberta pipe capacity, so the system had room and the barrel moved on schedule (site/api/balance.json, October 2026 forecast).

hops.name: Trunk: Trans Mountain, Edmonton to Westridge
hops.basis: ACTUAL (geometry, capacity and flows from the stack's CER-based network files; tolls are the filed tariff values in tolls.db)
hops.arrive_note: From Edmonton the barrel turns west on Trans Mountain: 1,147 kilometres through Hinton, Jasper, Kamloops and Hope to tidewater at Burnaby. This is the only pipeline in Canada that takes a heavy barrel straight to a tanker.
facts: The pipe path is the stack's own Trans Mountain network (builders/site/map_data/tmx_network.json): Edmonton (53.541, -113.365), Hinton, Jasper, Kamloops, Merritt, Hope, Port Kells, Burnaby, and the short dock leg to Westridge (49.2908, -122.95). The system is twinned: the original 1953 line plus the expansion line, 890 thousand barrels a day combined (tmx_network.json).

The flow the globe carries for this line: the egress network's Trans Mountain edge shows a latest CER flow of 819 thousand barrels a day for June 2026, against a proven floor of 865.6 thousand barrels a day (the highest monthly CER throughput the line has demonstrated; builders/site/map_data/egress_network.json). Marine loadings at Westridge itself ran 529.4 thousand barrels a day in June 2026 (CER Guide BB, in the Narrows stack's westridge_monthly.json). June 2026 is the latest CER month the stack holds for both figures.

THE TOLL PAID: Edmonton to Westridge, heavy crude, uncommitted, tank metered: C$14.06 a barrel (US$10.25 a barrel at the tariff database's conversion). Direct inject is C$13.93 a barrel (US$10.15). Filed in Trans Mountain Interim Tariff No. 123, issued Mar 31, 2026 and effective May 1, 2026, so it was the tariff in force when this barrel shipped (pipelines/tolls.db, tolls 185 and 186, path 34). The filed toll excludes the West Coast marine spill-response cargo fee, the capital assurance levy and the petroleum loss allowance, and a bid premium can apply in apportionment months at Westridge: those are real costs this stack does not print.

Time in the pipe: the tariff database's arb table carries a typical Edmonton to Burnaby transit of 10 days for this path (pipelines/tolls.db, arb_paths, Edmonton to Burnaby Trans Mountain path, labelled illustrative in that table).
The arb at this hop: the toll is the first priced leg of the Asia arc, US$10.25 a barrel. It is about two-fifths of what the ocean leg costs at the ride's dates, which is the next priced hop.

hops.name: Loading at Westridge: SEAWAYS REYES
hops.basis: ACTUAL (the Narrows AIS archive: the event pipeline's loading record and the vessel's own broadcast draught and destination)
hops.arrive_note: At the Westridge dock in Burrard Inlet the barrel is pumped aboard a real tanker whose loading the archive watched, hour by hour, in the third week of October 2026.
facts: The vessel is SEAWAYS REYES, MMSI 538007126, IMO 9779939, an Aframax tanker (AIS ship type 80). Her loading is a real record in the Narrows archive (workspace/narrows/events.jsonl), not a reconstruction.

She arrived at the Westridge berth box on Oct 19, 2026 at 21:22 UTC (15:22 Edmonton time), was alongside from 23:42 UTC, and sailed on Oct 21, 2026 at 21:52 UTC (15:52 Edmonton time): 48.5 hours alongside. The archive holds 309 of her position fixes between arrival and departure.

The loading shows in her draught, which is how the event pipeline calls a loading: she came in drawing 8.4 metres and left drawing 13.1 metres, a gain of 4.7 metres. That is the deepest draught gain of any clean Asia-bound loading in the archive's October window, tied with one other vessel, and her destination field never wavered.
Her broadcast destination, in her event record and in every outbound position fix, is CAVAN>CNYPG: Vancouver to Yangpu, China. CNYPG is the UN location code for Yangpu, on Hainan island.

Cargo size: the archive holds draught, not a cargo manifest, so no barrel count is printed as a fact. On the Baltic TD28 route basis this cargo prices on (an 80,000 tonne Aframax parcel), the parcel works out to roughly 530,000 to 550,000 barrels of dilbit. That range is a MODELLED estimate from the route's cargo basis, not an archive figure.

The arb at this hop: the ocean freight for this exact route, Vancouver to Ningbo on an Aframax (Baltic route TD28), was US$26.59 a barrel in the stack's latest held pull before loading, dated Oct 16, 2026 (lump sum US$15.59 million, time charter equivalent US$334,000 a day; Baltic Exchange via the digest goal's freight pull, freight_rates_weekly.csv). Freight at the ride's dates costs more than twice the pipeline toll.

hops.name: The crossing, part one: out of Burrard Inlet to the edge of watched water
hops.basis: ACTUAL (the vessel's real AIS track from the Narrows archive, decimated from 293 fixes to 147; every point in the track array is a real fix)
hops.arrive_note: This is the part of the crossing the archive can prove. The tanker threads Burrard Inlet, crosses the Strait of Georgia, runs down Haro Strait and out the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and the globe rides her actual track the whole way.
facts: The track in this hop is SEAWAYS REYES's actual AIS track: 293 position fixes from sailing at Westridge on Oct 21, 2026 at 21:52 UTC to the last fix on Oct 22, 2026 at 12:34 UTC, decimated to 147 points for the ride. No point is interpolated and none is drawn.

In that 14 hours 42 minutes she sailed 293.0 kilometres of track at a mean speed of 10.2 knots (fastest fix 13.4 knots): west out of Burrard Inlet, south across the Strait of Georgia, through Haro Strait, then west down the Strait of Juan de Fuca.

The last fix the archive holds is Oct 22, 2026 at 12:34 UTC (06:34 Edmonton time), at 48.518, -124.989, making 12.2 knots on a course of 272.5 degrees: due west, at sea speed, at the mouth of the strait.

The track ends there because the watching ends there. The Narrows collector watches three boxes (the Pacific Northwest, the California coast, and the St. Lawrence); its Pacific Northwest box ends at longitude -125.0, and the last fix sits 0.011 degrees inside that edge. The stack's separate global tanker collector held no positions at build time (its database was created Oct 27, 2026 and was still empty), so no offshore Pacific track exists in the stack for this vessel. The ride says so instead of drawing one.

Chokepoint context, stated honestly: there is no major chokepoint on the North Pacific run itself. The strait the barrel just used, Juan de Fuca, is a pilotage and traffic-separation waterway, not a PortWatch chokepoint, and the open-ocean great circle to North Asia passes no strait the PortWatch file tracks until the arrival-side waters at the far end (see the delivery hop).

The arb at this hop: nothing about the price changes while the ship is in watched water. What changes is exposure: from sailing to discharge the cargo is roughly three weeks of flat-price and freight risk that a Hardisty sale never carries. The closing hop prices that trade.

hops.name: The crossing, part two: the open Pacific (delivery leg)
hops.basis: MODELLED (a great-circle sailing estimate, drawn as an estimate. The archive holds no positions on this leg and the ride does not pretend otherwise)
hops.arrive_note: Past the edge of watched water the ride keeps going on the great circle, clearly labelled as an estimate, because a barrel ride that stops at the horizon would not be a ride. Nothing on this leg is an observed position.
facts: The great-circle distance from Westridge (49.2908, -122.95) to Yangpu, Hainan (19.74, 109.18) is about 10,779 kilometres. At a laden service speed of 11 to 12 knots that is roughly 20 to 22 days of sailing, which would put discharge in mid-November 2026, after the archive window this ride is built from. Both the line and the dates on this leg are a MODELLED estimate.

The standard North Pacific routing runs northwest past the Aleutian chain, then southwest down the East Asian coast. It crosses no Hormuz, no Malacca and no Panama: the three chokepoints that dominate tanker news are all on other oceans' routes, and none of them touches this barrel.

For scale on the arrival-side waters the stack does watch: on Oct 18, 2026, the latest day in the IMF PortWatch file the stack holds, the Korea Strait counted 47 tanker transits and the Bohai Strait 28 (hidden_files/datasets/global_barrels_ledger/portwatch_chokepoints_daily_2026.csv). Those are North China arrival waters, busy and moving normally. A Yangpu cargo approaches Hainan from the South China Sea side and does not need either strait; they are printed here as the nearest watched waters, not as gates this cargo passed.

The arb at this hop: the freight was fixed at loading-week levels (US$26.59 a barrel, Oct 16, 2026 pull). Every day of this leg, that fixed freight is either a bargain or a burden against whatever the Baltic prints next; the stack's freight pull is weekly, so the ride carries the Oct 16 print and labels it, rather than inventing a daily series.

hops.name: Delivery: Yangpu, Hainan
hops.basis: The destination is ACTUAL as the vessel's broadcast destination (her AIS destination field, held in the archive). The refinery named is the refinery that serves that port; that the cargo discharged into it specifically is ASSUMED, and the capacity figures are public data
hops.arrive_note: The barrel's broadcast destination is Yangpu, on the northwest coast of Hainan island, where Sinopec's Hainan refinery takes imported crude through its own deep-water terminal.
facts: Destination, as broadcast: Yangpu, China. The vessel's AIS destination field read CAVAN>CNYPG at her loading event and in every outbound fix the archive holds (workspace/narrows/events.jsonl and the positions archive). CNYPG is Yangpu's UN location code. This is the vessel's stated destination, which is the strongest destination evidence AIS gives; it is not a discharge confirmation, and the ride does not call it one.

The refinery at Yangpu is Sinopec's Hainan Refinery, in the Yangpu development zone, fed by a deep-water crude terminal in the Yangpu port area with 300,000 deadweight-tonne crude berths (public data: A Barrel Full's Hainan Refinery profile). Yangpu also hosts a Sinopec commercial crude storage base of about 16 million barrels, pipeline-connected to the refinery (public data: Sinopec via Oreanda News, Dec 2014).

Refinery capacity, from public data, stated as the range the public sources support: the plant was built at 160,000 barrels a day (8 million tonnes a year); an expansion to 13 million tonnes a year, about 261,000 barrels a day, won environmental approval in 2013 (Dow Jones via Hydrocarbon Processing, Feb 2013); GlobalData's refinery database lists its crude distillation unit at 185 thousand barrels a day (via Offshore Technology). The ride prints the range rather than picking the number that sounds best.

That this specific cargo discharged into the Hainan refinery (rather than into Yangpu storage or another Hainan receiver) is ASSUMED: Yangpu is the broadcast destination and the refinery is the port's crude receiver of scale, but the archive's evidence ends at the strait's mouth on Oct 22, 2026.

The arb at this hop: what the Yangpu buyer had to pay to make this cargo worth loading is priced in the closing hop. The delivered barrel competes in Asia against Middle East and Russian grades, and its break-even says how much room it had.

hops.name: The arb: what the Edmonton to Asia arc paid
hops.basis: MODELLED (an arithmetic stack of held components, each with its own date; the delivered Asia price itself is not held in the stack, so the arb is stated as a break-even, not as a claimed sale margin)
hops.arrive_note: The ride ends with the money. Every number below is a number this stack actually holds, with its date on it, and the one number the stack does not hold is named instead of invented.
facts: MODELLED break-even, components first. Pipeline toll, Edmonton to Westridge, heavy uncommitted: US$10.25 a barrel (C$14.06; Trans Mountain Interim Tariff No. 123, effective May 1, 2026; pipelines/tolls.db). Ocean freight, Vancouver to Ningbo, Aframax (Baltic TD28): US$26.59 a barrel (Oct 16, 2026, the latest TD28 print held when the vessel loaded; Baltic Exchange via the digest goal's freight pull). Transport stack, Edmonton to Asia: US$36.84 a barrel.

Origin value: on Oct 23, 2026, December 2026 WCS at Hardisty settled at US$28.50 under WTI on 555 traded lots (ICE TMW December 2026, the stack's ICE settlements file), and WTI settled at US$103.27 (the Oct 26, 2026 Now edition's record of Friday's settles). So a December barrel at Hardisty was worth about US$74.77.

Add the transport stack to the origin value and the delivered barrel in Asia had to clear about US$111.61 a barrel, which is WTI plus US$8.34, just to match selling the same barrel at Hardisty. That is the MODELLED break-even for this ride's arc at the ride's dates. During the loading window itself the differential was a touch narrower: December WCS settled at US$27.95 under WTI on Oct 20, 2026, on 569 traded lots.

What is not in that number, stated plainly: the Access Pipeline gathering toll (no filed tariff held), the Westridge marine charges and levies the TMX tariff excludes, pilotage, and any bid premium. All of them raise the true break-even above US$111.61. Financing is small by comparison: the arb table in tolls.db carries the standard financing note for a 10-day pipe transit, and the ocean leg's roughly three weeks is the larger carry.

What the stack cannot do, and does not: print the price this cargo actually sold at in Yangpu. No Asia delivered WCS assessment is held in the stack for October 2026, so the ride states the break-even the delivered price had to beat, with every component dated, instead of a margin it cannot support.

ghosts.episode_window: baseline H1 2025 – Jan/Feb 2026; episode from 2026-03-01 (JMIC counts 153 confirmed incidents since Mar 1); archive window scored Oct 1–25, 2026
ghosts.pattern_note: The fear-vs-physical gap is the pattern: the visible (AIS) layer collapsed to near zero while physical barrels recovered to most of pre-war by rerouting around the broken piece — dark, escorted shuttle and ship-to-ship relays through and around the strait, plus pipeline bypasses. Prices priced the visible break (Dated Brent above $120 on Oct 2 while ICE Brent sat near $101); the physical system priced a working, expensive workaround (TD3C earnings ~$1.37M/day Oct 16, war-risk premia 6–10% of hull value, VLCC round trips 12–15 days instead of ~4). Numeric ghost: supported (see arc).

arc_pattern.state_note: Normal: EIA put Hormuz flow at 20.9 mb/d in H1 2025 (~15 crude/condensate + ~5.5 products); PortWatch AIS tanker transits averaged 36.98/day in Jan–Feb 2026; bypass routes carried ~17% of non-Iranian Gulf crude

Break and workaround build: incidents accumulate (153 confirmed by Oct 18, JMIC); strait crude flow on Kpler's count fell to 9.75 mb/d in September; ~70%+ of strait crude was changing tankers off Fujairah/Oman by August; Iran's own loadings fell through the window (Mar ~2 mb/d → Jul ~740 kb/d → Aug 220–255 kb/d → Sep 0)

Physical recovery, visible collapse: AIS saw 0.44 transits/day (1.19% of pre-war count) while TankerTrackers counted >12 mb/d through the waterway in October (~70% of pre-war) and Kpler 11.7 mb/d (~82% of pre-war strait flow); total Gulf exports ex-Iran ran 24.5–24.6 mb/d in the week ending Oct 18, above the 23.3–24.4 pre-war level; bypass share ~40% of non-Iranian crude, up from 17%; VLCC exits averaged 32/week vs 36 pre-war; unescorted transits stayed single-digit per direction, US-assisted ~30/day

No normalization: attacks at a record pace for the war (UKMTO/JMIC through Oct 23), JMIC threat level SEVERE, Kharg still empty on satellite imagery — the recovery routes around the broken pieces; the waterway itself is not back

ghosts.source: goals/wcsb-s-d-model/hidden_files/hormuz_recheck_2026-10-25.md (full tier-1 audit, Oct 19–25 evidence) + goals/wcsb-s-d-model/hidden_files/datasets/world_watches/retired/hormuz.json (baseline sections, accessed 2026-09-23) + goals/wcsb-s-d-model/hidden_files/world_watches/additions_2026-10-04/hormuz.json (Oct 2 Kpler/East-West figures)

ghosts.pattern_note: A terminal going to zero in steps while its floating storage drains: loadings stepped down month by month, offshore floating storage (~135 Mbbl off Malaysia/Singapore at the outbreak) discharged to zero by mid-October and could not be refilled, and the berths then stood empty for ~40 days on satellite imagery — the longest dormancy gap is 3 days between images against a 24–48 h VLCC load time, so the emptiness is observed, not inferred. Narrative-plus-numbers ghost: the step-down figures are tracker estimates (Kpler/Vortexa via wires) carried in the archive, not stack-measured volumes.

arc_pattern.state_note: Iran loaded ~2 mb/d in March, falling to ~740 kb/d in July (Reuters-cited Kpler/Vortexa, Sep 1)
~220–255 kb/d loaded in August — while the AIS export series at Kharg already read zero (see Silence layer)
Zero loadings in September — the first zero month since the war began on Bloomberg/Kpler/Vortexa estimates alike; at least 11 laden tankers anchored east of Kharg, bottled up

No resumption: Bloomberg's Sentinel-1/2 imagery review (~Oct 19) found crude berths empty through ~40 days of dormancy; floating storage fully discharged to zero by mid-October (Kpler via WSJ, Oct 21)

ghosts.source: goals/wcsb-s-d-model/hidden_files/hormuz_recheck_2026-10-25.md section 3b + goals/wcsb-s-d-model/hidden_files/datasets/world_watches/retired/iran.json (floating-storage sections: ~135 Mbbl end-July broad measure → ~107 Mbbl Aug 26 → ~86 Mbbl on the water Sep 30)

ghosts.hotspot: Red Sea / Yanbu — the bypass that became a target
ghosts.pattern_note: The reroute inherits the risk: as Hormuz barrels shifted to the East-West pipeline and Yanbu, the bypass itself was struck — a projectile hit inside Yanbu port on Oct 1 (first reported strike inside the port, loading temporarily suspended) and Aramco's Riyadh facility was struck Oct 3. Insurance repriced the bypass before volumes stopped: Yanbu war-risk premiums rose to ~3% of vessel value from below 1% in early July, southern ports quoted as high as 7%. Narrative ghost: the archive supports dates and the premium/volume figures below, but no day-by-day flow series, so no numeric arc beyond those points.

arc_pattern.state_note: Bypass share ~17% of non-Iranian Gulf crude left without crossing Hormuz (Kpler via WSJ, as archived)

Aramco notified October Yanbu loadings near 2 mb/d (Reuters/trade sources); Kpler estimated East-West/Yanbu flows could reach 3–4 mb/d within days, and later put East-West pipeline flows at almost 6 mb/d with ~4.5 mb/d available for Red Sea exports
Strike inside Yanbu port Oct 1 suspends crude loading temporarily; Houthi strike on Aramco Riyadh facility Oct 3; Yanbu war-risk ~3% of hull value (from <1% in early July)
Watch retired into the Middle East / Hormuz watches; Yemeni government announced a Saudi-led operation to retake Houthi-held territory (Oct 4 reporting)

ghosts.pattern_note: Narrative pattern only — the archive is a dated news-bullet watch, not a flow series, so the numeric ghost awaits more archive. Pattern the bullets support: repeated named strikes on refineries/petrochemical plants deep inside Russia (Ryazan was the last known refinery incident, overnight Oct 16; Omsk petrochemical plant struck Oct 24, >2,500 km from Ukraine), then a pause of more than a week in refinery strikes by Oct 24 alongside a negotiated diesel-export arrangement (three Russian diesel tankers bound for North America reported Oct 23–26) and a stated conditional offer (Oct 26) to stop refinery strikes if Russia stops attacking Ukraine's power grid. Pin is an illustrative central-Russia placement, not an in-stack coordinate; named-plant coordinates are not in the watch file.

arc_pattern.state_note: Strike phase in the archive: refinery incidents continue, last known at Ryazan overnight Oct 16
Strike pause: no refinery strikes for more than a week by Oct 24 (SFG Media via the watch); long-range strikes continue on other targets (Omsk, Oct 24)

Export/negotiation turn: Russian diesel tankers reported heading to North America under a Putin–Trump arrangement (Reuters/LSEG Oct 23; TankerTrackers via Robban Assafina Oct 26); Zelensky's conditional refinery-strike halt offer reported Oct 26

fields.name: Leduc-Woodbend
fields.discovery_note: Imperial Oil's Leduc No. 1 blew in on February 13, 1947, after 133 consecutive dry holes in western Canada, and opened the Devonian reef era.
fields.operator_today: Tenaz Energy (largest operator, 87.5% WI in the main Leduc-Woodbend asset); multiple small operators
fields.crude_character: Light sweet crude from Devonian Leduc (D3) and Woodbend reefs, roughly 39-40 API; today also shallower Cretaceous (Rex, Sparky, Glauconite, Ellerslie) oil

series.basis: Rate at end of 1947, about 30 wells producing (Canadian Encyclopedia, City of Leduc entry)
Annual production 4,657,371 bbl, Alberta Petroleum and Natural Gas Conservation Board table reproduced in Breen (1993)
Annual production 9,688,784 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Annual production 10,589,466 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Annual production 13,743,118 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Floor value: field published as producing 'over 20 million barrels annually between 1953 and 1956' (Wikipedia, Leduc No. 1, citing field history); 20M bbl/yr = 54.8 kb/d
Tenaz Energy Leduc-Woodbend production, Q3 2025: 2,326 boe/d (barrels of oil equivalent, roughly 65% oil) - Tenaz corporate presentation, Nov 2025

current.source: Tenaz Energy corporate presentation (Nov 2025), Q3 2025 Leduc-Woodbend output 2,326 boe/d

fields.life_note: Leduc No. 1 (1947) proved Devonian reefs could hold giant oil pools and started Alberta's modern oil age. The field passed 20 million barrels a year in 1953-1956, produced over 250 million barrels in its first 50 years, and then settled into a long stripper-well decline. It still produces today: Tenaz Energy now develops the shallower Cretaceous zones above the old reef with horizontal wells.

fields.name: Redwater
fields.discovery_note: Imperial Oil discovered the Redwater Leduc D3 reef in October 1948, Alberta's second Devonian giant and for a time Canada's most prolific oil field.
fields.operator_today: Conifer Energy (principal operator of the Redwater Leduc pool)
fields.crude_character: Light crude from a Devonian Leduc D3 limestone reef with a very strong natural water drive; produced water cut is now extreme (historically over 100 bbl of water per barrel of oil)

series.basis: Annual production 36,875 bbl (Oct-Dec only), Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Annual production 4,793,491 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Annual production 10,745,538 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Annual production 23,177,607 bbl, Conservation Board table in Breen (1993)
Peak production year: 'Production peaked at about 180,000 barrels/day in 1975' - Polczer (1998), Journal of Canadian Petroleum Technology, via OSTI/ETDE
Polczer (1998): declined to about 6,600 bbl/d in 1998; cumulative 816 million bbl of 852 million recoverable by then
Conifer Energy operations page (accessed Oct 2026): 2,650 boe/d, 92% oil, through 280 wells

Petrinex public volumetrics, in-stack (wcsb.duckdb, petrinex_vol_panel): author's aggregation of 2025 PROD oil+condensate volumes over facilities whose names contain the field name - an approximate footprint, not the AER field boundary (102 Redwater-named facilities; wider than Conifer's operated Leduc pool, which it reports at 2,650 boe/d)

current.source: Conifer Energy, Redwater operations page (2,650 boe/d, 92% oil)

fields.life_note: Found in 1948, Redwater was drilled up on 40-acre spacing by 1955 (925 wells) over a 1.3-billion-barrel reef, and a powerful natural water drive kept it growing for decades to a peak near 180,000 bbl/d in 1975. The same water drive then drowned it: by 1998 it made about 6,600 bbl/d alongside the world's largest salt-water disposal operation. Conifer Energy now runs it at roughly 2,650 boe/d and promotes it as a CO2-EOR candidate.
sources: Breen (1993), Table 5.5
Polczer, S. (1998), 'Redwater fifty years later', JCPT, via OSTI/ETDE abstract

fields.name: Pembina (Cardium)
fields.discovery_note: The Socony-Seaboard Pembina No. 1 well found oil in the Cretaceous Cardium sandstone near Drayton Valley in 1953, opening Canada's largest conventional oil field by area and oil in place.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Obsidian Energy, Whitecap Resources, Canadian Natural Resources, Bonterra and many others)
fields.crude_character: Light sweet crude, about 38-40 API, from the shallow Cardium sandstone and conglomerate; a stratigraphic trap with solution-gas drive and no natural water leg

series.basis: Peak month-rate year: 4.5 million bbl/month in 1970 (GeoScout monthly pool data, in Parkes et al., Pembina Cardium reservoir evaluation)
Field low point of 600,000 bbl/month in 2010 before horizontal wells (Parkes et al., GeoScout data)
Study states the pool was 'currently producing approximately 1.9 million barrels of oil per month' after the horizontal/multistage-frac revival; study dated by its 2011-2013 references to about 2014

current.source: Parkes, Makowski & Bilyk, Reservoir Evaluation and Hydrocarbon Play Assessment of the Cardium Formation - Pembina Field (GeoScout pool data); Hart Energy separately reports the field peaked at about 200,000 boe/d (oil equivalent, including gas) in the early 1970s

fields.life_note: Pembina is a giant sand wedge that pinches out into shale: about 7.8-9.4 billion barrels in place, but thin and tight, so primary recovery was under 10% and waterflooding from the late 1950s did the heavy lifting to a 1970 peak near 148,000 bbl/d of oil. It declined for four decades to about 20,000 bbl/d, then horizontal wells with multistage fracturing from 2009 gave the old field a second life, roughly tripling output. Cumulative production passed 1.3 billion barrels, only about 15% of the oil in place.
sources: Parkes et al., Pembina Cardium reservoir evaluation (bradleyparkes.com), GeoScout monthly data from 1963
Hart Energy (2012), 'Cardium Full Circle'
Nightingale et al. (2009), Energy Procedia 1: Pembina Cardium CO2 Monitoring Project site description

fields.name: Swan Hills
fields.discovery_note: Home Oil's Regent Swan Hills 8-11-68-10W5 well found oil in the Devonian Beaverhill Lake (Swan Hills) carbonate in 1957, the largest conventional carbonate oil field in Canada.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Obsidian Energy and Razor Energy hold major Swan Hills unit interests)
fields.crude_character: Light sweet crude, about 40-42 API, from Devonian Swan Hills Formation reef build-ups and platform carbonates

series.basis: East Swan Hills Unit only: peak oil production 1,959 m3/d in 1969 (JCPT, East Swan Hills Unit waterflood optimization study)

Swan Hills Unit #1 only (about 80% of the pool's oil in place): 27,000 bbl/d reported in CSEG Recorder, 'Swan Hills Unit #1: Adding Value with Seismic' (Home Oil era, circa 2000); cumulative 540M bbl to that date
One operator's share only: Razor Energy Swan Hills assets averaged 2,456 boe/d in Q3 2023 (Razor MD&A, via court affidavit, Feb 2024)

Petrinex public volumetrics, in-stack (wcsb.duckdb, petrinex_vol_panel): author's aggregation of 2025 PROD oil+condensate volumes over facilities whose names contain the field name - an approximate footprint, not the AER field boundary (50 Swan Hills-named facilities)

current.source: Petrinex Alberta volumetrics, in-stack aggregation over Swan Hills-named facilities (2025 average); cross-check: Razor Energy's Swan Hills share alone was 2,456 boe/d in Q3 2023

fields.life_note: Swan Hills came on production once a pipeline arrived in 1959-1962, was unitized in 1963, waterflooded from 1965 and then hydrocarbon-miscible flooded from 1985 - one of Canada's flagship enhanced-recovery projects. The Beaverhill Lake A and B pools held about 2.9 billion barrels in place and had produced about 0.9 billion barrels by end-2010. Today the field runs at very high water cut (about 97% water in the south unit), and its hot produced water now also drives a geothermal power plant.

fields.name: Judy Creek
fields.discovery_note: Imperial Oil discovered the Judy Creek Beaverhill Lake reef in February 1959, a few miles south of Swan Hills, and it became the proving ground for Canadian miscible flooding.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Obsidian Energy operates the main Beaverhill Lake units, inherited from Imperial via Pengrowth)
fields.crude_character: Light crude, about 41 API, from an atoll-like Devonian Swan Hills Formation reef about 115 km2 in area

series.basis: Annual production of 5 million bbl in 1963 from the Judy Creek Swan Hills bank, 169 producing wells in 1964 (Bulletin of Canadian Petroleum Geology, Judy Creek carbonate bank study)

current.source: Bulletin of Canadian Petroleum Geology (1965) - the only metered field rate found in public sources; see notes: no reliable recent field-total rate was found

fields.life_note: Judy Creek was unitized and put on peripheral water injection within four years of its 1959 discovery, one of the fastest, most deliberate developments of its era, and Imperial reported a pool productivity potential of 100,000 bbl/d in the mid-1970s. A pattern waterflood replaced the peripheral flood in 1974, and in 1985 Esso started a first-contact hydrocarbon miscible flood that became a textbook Canadian EOR project. The reef still produces under Obsidian Energy and smaller operators, alongside newer Pekisko and Beaverhill Lake horizontal drilling.
sources: JCPT, 'Development of Judy Creek - A Case Study' (Imperial Oil)
Flewitt (1974), SPWLA: Judy Creek BHL 'A' Pool 'current potential productivity of 100,000 BOPD, 188 active wells' (peak field here is this published potential, not a metered rate)
JCPT (1993), 'Solvent Tracers and the Judy Creek Hydrocarbon Miscible Flood'
Bulletin of Canadian Petroleum Geology 14(1): Swan Hills Member at Judy Creek (1963 production, 1964 well count)

fields.name: Mitsue / Nipisi (Slave Lake)
fields.discovery_note: The Mitsue Gilwood field was discovered in 1964 south of Slave Lake, opening the Nipisi-Mitsue Gilwood sand trend that holds more than 500 million barrels of oil in place.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Canadian Natural Resources operates Nipisi; Tamarack Valley and others are active in the Slave Lake / Clearwater area)
fields.crude_character: Light oil from Middle Devonian Gilwood sandstones (Mitsue) and Slave Point / Beaverhill Lake carbonates (Nipisi); the wider Slave Lake area also produces heavier Clearwater oil

series.basis: One owner's properties only: Penn West's Greater Mitsue assets produced 4,500 boe/d (78% liquids) in H1 2015, per its sale announcement
Nipisi field only: oil production 2.34 million bbl in 2020 (Global Energy Monitor, from AER data)
Nipisi field only: oil production 7.55 million bbl in 2022 (Global Energy Monitor, from AER data), lifted by the Clearwater revival around Slave Lake

Petrinex public volumetrics, in-stack (wcsb.duckdb, petrinex_vol_panel): author's aggregation of 2025 PROD oil+condensate volumes over facilities whose names contain the field name - an approximate footprint, not the AER field boundary (12 Mitsue-named facilities - the old Gilwood pool batteries)

Petrinex public volumetrics, in-stack (wcsb.duckdb, petrinex_vol_panel): author's aggregation of 2025 PROD oil+condensate volumes over facilities whose names contain the field name - an approximate footprint, not the AER field boundary (56 Nipisi-named facilities; includes the Clearwater multilateral batteries around Nipisi/Marten Hills, a wider footprint than GEM's Nipisi field definition)

current.source: Petrinex Alberta volumetrics, in-stack aggregation over Nipisi-named facilities (2025 average, incl. Clearwater batteries)

fields.life_note: Mitsue (1964) and neighbouring Nipisi (1963) produce from Gilwood sands draped over a salt-dissolution trap south and north of Slave Lake; the ERCB's 1968 reserves review already credited Mitsue Gilwood A with 340 million barrels in place and a big enhanced-recovery uplift. The old pools declined into stripper status, but Slave Lake is busy again: Nipisi output roughly tripled between 2020 and 2022 as operators chased the Clearwater play with multilateral wells. The peak field here is simply the highest sourced point - the Gilwood pools' 1960s-1970s peak rate was not found in published sources.

fields.name: Rainbow
fields.discovery_note: Banff Oil and Aquitaine's Rainbow 7-32-109-8W6 well hit 435 feet of oil pay in a Keg River reef in February 1965, a discovery big enough to make the front page of the New York Times financial section.
fields.operator_today: Cenovus Energy (operator of the Rainbow and Rainbow South fields)
fields.crude_character: Light oil, 38.7 API at the discovery well, from Middle Devonian Keg River pinnacle reefs and platform dolomites; some pools are sour

series.basis: Rainbow field oil production 1.19 million bbl in 2020 (Global Energy Monitor, from AER data); cumulative oil to 2019 was 723 million bbl
Rainbow field oil production 0.77 million bbl in 2022 (Global Energy Monitor, from AER data)

Petrinex public volumetrics, in-stack (wcsb.duckdb, petrinex_vol_panel): author's aggregation of 2025 PROD oil+condensate volumes over facilities whose names contain the field name - an approximate footprint, not the AER field boundary (10 Rainbow-named facilities; agrees with the AER-based GEM figure of 2.1 kb/d for 2022)

current.source: Petrinex Alberta volumetrics, in-stack aggregation over Rainbow-named facilities (2025 average)

fields.life_note: Rainbow was a winter-only frontier in 1965 - 100 miles of frozen bush road, Hercules airlifts, wells on 640-acre spacing that could flow 5,000 bbl/d - and within a few years about 45 reefs had added over a billion barrels of recoverable oil to Alberta's books. Waterfloods began in 1968 and hydrocarbon miscible floods followed in nine reefs, among the earliest in Alberta. The sub-basin has produced more than 1.1 billion barrels; the oil rate is now small (about 2,000 bbl/d in 2022) and Cenovus runs the area mainly for gas, with oilfield brine now also eyed for lithium. No published historical peak rate for the field was found - the peak shown is the highest point in the sourced modern series, not the field's true 1970s peak.
sources: Last, G.J., 'Development of the Rainbow area', API conference paper, via OSTI (discovery, 45 reefs, >1B bbl recoverable, 5,000 bpd wells)
BOE Report (2023), 'Well of the Week - All the colours of the rainbow'

fields.name: Zama
fields.discovery_note: The same 1965 Banff-Aquitaine Keg River discovery program that found Rainbow opened the Zama pinnacle-reef play further north; Zama-area pools were found and developed from 1965 through 1969.
fields.operator_today: Paramount Resources (acquired Apache Canada, the long-time Zama operator, in 2017)
fields.crude_character: Light oil from small, steep Keg River pinnacle reefs, with sour associated gas (H2S) that later made the field a pioneer site for acid-gas injection and CO2 storage

series.basis: Liquids production of Phillips Petroleum's Zama-area assets (6,000 bbl/d of liquid hydrocarbons plus 70 MMcf/d of gas) at Apache's acquisition, Oil & Gas Journal, Dec 2000

current.source: Oil & Gas Journal (2000), Apache acquisition of Phillips' Zama assets - the only field-area rate found in public sources; no reliable recent field-total rate was found

fields.life_note: Zama City exists because of the 1965-1969 Keg River pinnacle discoveries in Alberta's far northwest muskeg: hundreds of small, tall reefs, each a separate little pool, developed by a rotating cast of operators and consolidated by Apache Canada in 2000-2001. From 2006 Apache ran a pioneering acid-gas EOR and storage project in the Zama F Pool, injecting CO2 and H2S that would otherwise be flared or vented. Paramount Resources took over the area with its 2017 Apache Canada acquisition; the field's early peak rate does not appear in the public sources found.
sources: Alberta Historic Places, 'Zama' (oil fields discovered 1965-1969)
Oil & Gas Journal (2000), 'Apache to acquire Phillips' Zama assets in Alberta'

Paramount Resources 2017 annual report (Apache Canada acquisition)

fields.name: Peace River
fields.discovery_note: Shell Canada began producing bitumen from its Peace River oil sands leases in 1979 with the Peace River In Situ Project, a thermal pilot on some of the heaviest oil in Alberta.
fields.operator_today: Canadian Natural Resources (acquired Shell's Peace River Complex and Cliffdale in 2017)
fields.crude_character: Extra-heavy bitumen, about 7.5 API, from the Bluesky/Gething sands - too thick to flow cold at reservoir conditions in the thermal area, while nearby Cliffdale produces cold with horizontal wells

series.basis: Peace River Expansion Project (PREP) demonstration plant rate of 12,600 bbl/d at start-up in 1986 (Shell Carmon Creek brochure) - design/demonstration rate, not a metered annual average
Peace River Complex producing about 12,000 bbl/d in 2006 (Petroleum News, Dec 2006); the plant's licence was 12,500 bbl/d annual average
Shell's Peace River properties at CNRL's acquisition: Peace River Complex thermal about 5,400 bbl/d plus Cliffdale cold production about 8,400 bbl/d (CNRL acquisition announcement, Mar 2017)

current.source: Canadian Natural Resources acquisition announcement, March 9 2017 (13,800 bbl/d from the 100%-owned Peace River properties)

fields.life_note: Peace River was Shell's forty-year thermal experiment: a 1979 pilot, a 12,600 bbl/d demonstration plant in 1986 (today's Peace River Complex), and decades of work on steam drive and horizontal-well variations of cyclic steam in 7.5-API bitumen. Shell's giant Carmon Creek expansion (80,000 bbl/d) was approved in 2013 but cancelled in 2015, and CNRL bought the complex and the neighbouring Cliffdale cold-heavy field in 2017. Output has stayed in the low tens of thousands of barrels a day - a science project that never became a giant.
sources: Shell Canada, Carmon Creek project brochure (PRISP 1979; PREP 12,600 bbl/d in 1986)
Petroleum News (Dec 24 2006), 'Peace River enters big leagues'
Canadian Natural Resources / GlobeNewswire (Mar 9 2017), AOSP and Peace River acquisition

fields.name: Cold Lake
fields.discovery_note: Imperial Oil began testing cyclic steam stimulation at Ethel Lake in the Cold Lake deposit in 1964, after evaluation drilling from 1962; the deposit itself had been delineated by drilling in the late 1950s.
fields.operator_today: Imperial Oil (the Cold Lake entry is Imperial's operation; Canadian Natural and Cenovus produce elsewhere in the Cold Lake deposit)
fields.crude_character: Bitumen of about 10 API from the Lower Cretaceous Clearwater Formation, produced by cyclic steam stimulation ('huff and puff') and, at Grand Rapids, steam-assisted gravity drainage

series.basis: Pilot plant rate: Cold Lake began as a 10,000 bbl/d pilot in 1975 (Oil Sands Magazine, Imperial Cold Lake history)
Imperial was producing an average of 90,000 bbl/d by 1991 (Daily Commercial News / ConstructConnect history of Cold Lake and GCOS)
EUB data for 2000: 119,000 bbl/d for Imperial Oil Cold Lake (Alberta CHOPS report, 2002)
About 24,000 m3/d (150,000 bbl/d) circa 2010, with cumulative production over 1 billion bbl by end-2010 (IPTC paper, EarthDoc)
Imperial Oil 2024 annual results: Cold Lake production averaged 148,000 bbl/d in 2024

current.source: Imperial Oil 2024 annual financial statements / Q4 2024 release (Cold Lake averaged 148,000 bbl/d)

fields.life_note: Cold Lake is the granddaddy of in-situ oil sands: Imperial piloted cyclic steam here from 1964, shelved a $13-billion megaproject in 1981, and instead built the field in small phases from 1985 - a template the whole industry later copied. Five plants (Leming, Maskwa, Mahihkan, Mahkeses, Nabiye) and thousands of wells have produced well over a billion barrels of 10-API bitumen. Output has held near 150,000 bbl/d for over a decade, most recently 148,000 bbl/d in 2024 with the Grand Rapids SAGD project offsetting CSS decline.
sources: Oil Sands Magazine, 'Imperial pivots on Cold Lake expansion plans' (1975 pilot, 1985 commercial start)
ConstructConnect / Daily Commercial News (2017), 'How Sun Oil and Imperial Oil built an oilsands energy powerhouse' (90,000 bbl/d by 1991)
Alberta CHOPS report (2002), EUB 2000 data

fields.name: Athabasca Oil Sands (mining)
fields.discovery_note: Great Canadian Oil Sands (now Suncor) opened the first commercial oil sands mine north of Fort McMurray in 1967 at 45,000 bbl/d; the bitumen itself had been seen by Europeans since Peter Pond in 1778 and used by First Nations for centuries.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Suncor, Syncrude, Canadian Natural Resources, Imperial Oil at Kearl)
fields.crude_character: Surface-mined bitumen, roughly 8-10 API, most of it upgraded on site into synthetic crude oil of about 30+ API

series.basis: GCOS nameplate capacity at opening, 45,000 bbl/d (House of Commons RNNR committee report; BOE Report oil sands timeline)
Total Alberta oil sands production rate in the year Syncrude opened (UBC MINE 292 lecture series, 'Oil Sands Mining and Processing'); at this date all oil sands production was mined
Total Alberta oil sands production rate (same UBC lecture series); predominantly mined, with the first small Cold Lake in-situ volumes from 1985

In-stack AER ST39 mined-bitumen table, annual average
In-stack AER ST39 mined-bitumen table, annual average (the same table's 2024 value, 1,714 kb/d, checks against AER ST98's published 1,720.5 kb/d for 2024)

fields.life_note: Mining started as a gamble: GCOS's 45,000 bbl/d plant in 1967 was called the biggest private investment in Canadian history, and Syncrude's dragline mine followed in 1978 after governments took equity to save it. Truck-and-shovel mining, then the 2000s boom (Horizon, Jackpine, Kearl, Fort Hills), turned it into an industry that passed a million barrels a day of mined bitumen in 2014. It is still growing slowly by debottlenecking existing mines - 1.77 million bbl/d in 2025 - and the peak is simply the latest year.

fields.name: Lloydminster (heavy oil belt)
fields.discovery_note: The first Lloydminster oil well was completed in 1938 on the Saskatchewan side of the border city, though commercial production only began in 1943-1945 and Husky Oil's arrival in 1946 made the field.
fields.operator_today: multiple (Cenovus Energy is the largest operator, including the Lloydminster thermal projects and upgrader; Canadian Natural and many juniors also produce)
fields.crude_character: Heavy oil of 11-18 API from shallow, unconsolidated Mannville sands; produced cold with sand (CHOPS) for decades and increasingly by thermal (SAGD-style) projects since the 2010s

series.basis: Field producing almost 3,000,000 bbl/yr by 1955 from over 700 wells (JCPT, 'The Lloydminster Heavy Oil Area')
Production from the Lloydminster area reached a new high of 13,900 bbl/d in 1970 (Husky Oil 1970 annual report)
Husky-operated Lloydminster properties at approximately 27,500 bbl/d in 1977 (Husky Oil 1977 annual report)

Cenovus only: Lloydminster thermal projects 103,000 bbl/d plus Lloydminster conventional 17,000 bbl/d in 2023 (Cenovus 2024 budget coverage, Pipeline Online); other operators add more, so this understates the area total

current.source: Cenovus Energy 2024 capital budget (Lloydminster thermal 103 kb/d + conventional 17 kb/d in 2023), via Pipeline Online

fields.life_note: Lloydminster heavy oil was a local asphalt-and-bunker-fuel business from the 1940s - Husky built its refinery here in 1947 - and stayed small for decades because the oil barely flows and markets were thin. The Lloydminster and Regina upgraders (1992) and then CHOPS cold production in the 1990s turned the belt into a major producer, and Cenovus's thermal projects have pushed the area's output to record levels this decade. The peak shown is a floor: it counts Cenovus alone in 2023.
sources: JCPT (1973), 'The Lloydminster Heavy Oil Area'

fields.name: Ghawar
fields.discovery_note: Aramco's Ain Dar No. 1 found oil in 1948 in what proved to be a single 280-by-30 km Jurassic carbonate field, the largest conventional oil field on Earth.
fields.crude_character: Arab Light crude, about 33-34 API, from the Jurassic Arab-D carbonate reservoir, produced with peripheral water injection since the 1960s

series.basis: Output in the field's first year on stream, 126,000 bbl/d (Oil & Gas Journal data compiled in Sorkhabi 2010)
1975 output 4.2 million bbl/d (Oil & Gas Journal data compiled in Sorkhabi 2010)
Peak production 5.7 million bbl/d in 1981 (Saudi Aramco 2019 bond prospectus, reported by Oil & Gas News and NS Energy)
Midpoint of the published range: Ghawar produced 2.5-3.0 million bbl/d during 1982-1990 as Saudi output was cut back (Sorkhabi 2010, citing OGJ data)
Midpoint of the published range: 4.6-5.2 million bbl/d reported for 1993-2003 by Aramco geologist A.M. Afifi (AAPG Distinguished Lecture 2004, via Sorkhabi 2010)
Maximum sustainable capacity of 3.8 million bbl/d at Dec 31, 2018 (Saudi Aramco bond prospectus, April 2019) - a capacity figure, not a metered production rate

current.source: Saudi Aramco bond prospectus (April 2019), maximum sustainable capacity 3.8 million bbl/d; also Wikipedia, Ghawar Field infobox (current production 3.8M bbl/d, year 2019)

fields.life_note: Ghawar came on stream in 1951 and by the 1970s was the swing field of the world oil market, peaking at 5.7 million bbl/d in 1981 before Saudi Arabia cut output in the 1980s and Ghawar settled into a 4.5-5 million bbl/d plateau through the 1990s. Aramco's 2019 bond prospectus ended decades of secrecy: maximum sustainable capacity had slipped to 3.8 million bbl/d. It has still produced more than half of all the oil Saudi Arabia has ever pumped.

Wikipedia, 'Ghawar Field' (coordinates, discovery, current production)

fields.name: Burgan (Greater Burgan)
fields.discovery_note: Kuwait Oil Company's Burgan No. 1 struck oil in February 1938 in Cretaceous sandstones so prolific the field is still the world's largest sandstone oil field.
fields.crude_character: Medium crude, about 30-32 API, from Cretaceous Wara and Burgan sandstones with a strong natural water drive

series.basis: Production reached 344,000 bbl/d by 1950 from 99 wells (field history compiled in Grokipedia, citing KOC-based references)
First reached 1 million bbl/d in 1955 (Simmons, 'The World's Giant Oilfields', and field histories)
Reached 2 million bbl/d by 1968 (Simmons, giant oilfields compilation)
Peak of 2,415,068 bbl/d in 1972 (field production histories; IPTC paper gives 'around 2,400,000 bbl/d' for the 1972 peak)
Production halted entirely during the 1990-1991 Iraqi invasion and occupation; wells were sabotaged and set ablaze (IPTC 17617 field history)
Declined to around 1,700,000 bbl/d by 2005 (IPTC 17617, citing Croft 2013 and Cordahi & Critchlow 2005)
620.5 million boe in 2023, about 1.7 million bbl/d of hydrocarbons (Global Energy Monitor, Burgan field page)

current.source: Global Energy Monitor, Burgan Oil and Gas Field page (2023 production 620.5M boe/yr)

fields.life_note: Burgan was commercial from 1946 and for a quarter-century was the most productive field on Earth, passing a million barrels a day in 1955 and peaking at 2.41 million bbl/d in 1972. In 1991 retreating Iraqi forces set its wells on fire and production stopped dead; Kuwait rebuilt it within a few years. KOC now holds Greater Burgan near 1.7 million bbl/d with waterflooding, infill drilling and digital-field management.

Simmons & Co., 'The World's Giant Oilfields' (1955 and 1968 milestones, 2.41M bbl/d 1972 peak)
